As Sam said, the chances are starting to come for Arsenal now, with Timber lifting a cross straight on to the head of Merino but he failed to generate enough power and his effort was straight at the goalkeeper.

Madueke drops a shoulder to make room for a right-footed cross, but his delivery is over hit. Mikel Merino is playing in the Odegaard role tonight, but is not as nimble footed as the Arsenal captain.

That is Arsenal’s best chance so far though! Loose ball picked up and Timber released on the overlap, and it was a good pull-back to pick out Bruno Guimaraes but he fired wide.

There’s a goal coming here, and it’s going to be scored by Arsenal. They are finding gaps between the Lille lines and getting into some extremely dangerous positions in the inside channels. It feels like a matter of time.

David Raya gathers a cross after good defending from Timber, but then the Arsenal goalkeeper almost does a Shay Given against Dion Dublin at the edge of the box, but Rice put his foot in to get Raya out of bother. There was a frantic cry of “man on!” from the Arsenal crowd.

Lewis-Skelly and Madueke both deliver crosses into the Lille penalty area but they are repelled. Arsenal lacking some familiarity with their combinations off the flanks so far, but Eze does well to burst past his man to tee up Guimaraes but the shot is blocked.

Arsenal fail to make the most of a wide free-kick, before Bruno G elicits a cheer from the crowd when he slides into a tackle at the expense of a throw in. With Lewis-Skelly at left-back and Eze in front of him, there is not much natural width on the Arsenal left.

Bentaleb, the former Spurs midfielder, puts his head up to pick out the stretching run of Ueda, but the Lille forward lacked support and the moved fizzled out. It’s been quite a tidy start from the French side.

From Czechia sub at Wembley last week, Ondrej Zmrzly, a man with no vowels in his surname, to tonight and Lille sub Soriba Diaoune who has the full set in his.

End-to-end football for a couple of minutes. Madueke with a cute reverse pass into Merino inside the box but it broke down for Arsenal, before Lille launched a dangerous counter-attack through on-loan Forest attacker Bakwa, who cut inside and let fly. Great block from Gabriel.

Madueke did some encouraging things against Leeds but has been a bit untidy so far, slipping and handling the ball before miscuing an attempted pass towards Timber on the overlap.

Then Lille do well to play out from deep and work the ball into midfield but Andre gives away a sloppy pass.

Both teams enjoying a feel of the ball in the opening exchanges, and there is some good work in a tight space down the right from Konsa and Timber but Madueke could not take the ball with him.

Arsenal then start to establish some dominance in the Lille half, moving the ball from side to side.

Lille get the game under way at the Emirates.

Declan Rice captains Arsenal. Were it not for Martin Zubimendi sustaining a knock in the post-Leeds warm down, Rice may well have been on the bench with Saka, Odegaard and Havertz.

Arsenal’s right-back has looked quite rusty on his fleeting appearances so far this season, searching for rhythm after a pretty serious groin problem. He pushed himself to appear in the Champions League final and subsequently missed the World Cup.

I would expect him to play like a third centre-back at times, allowing Lewis-Skelly to drift into midfield from left-back. That role might also help Timber preserve his legs.

It had escaped my attention that Arsenal defender Gabriel is facing his former club tonight. At £27m, signed in 2020, he has to go down as one of Arteta’s best signings, and one of the best value signings any Premier League club has made this decade.

It’s very difficult. You come across very special people in life and Ken was certainly one of them. He’s an absolute legend of this football club. I think he’s the soul of this football club and someone that has given his life to this club.

This stadium wouldn’t be built if not for him. So, very sad news. The legacy he’s leaving is immense and our thoughts are with his family and we want to pay a proper tribute when we can.

Our players will be wearing black armbands this evening in memory of Ken Friar OBE. Rest in peace, Ken ❤️ https://t.co/xf91JABjrD

Lille’s manager is Davide Ancelotti, the son of Carlo, and you would assume he has picked up a few tips and tricks from his dad about success in this competition. Carlo, after all, has won the European Cup on five separate occasions. This is Davide’s second job as a manager, following a spell at Brazilian side Botafogo.

Some of Bukayo Saka’s finishing has been wayward so far this season, but the volume of chances coming his way bodes well. At this fledgling stage of the season, only Erling Haaland is averaging more non-penalty expected goals per 90 minutes in the Premier League.

As Sam Dean explores in this piece, Arteta seems to be encouraging Saka to take up more central positions inside the box.

Sam writes: “Is Saka becoming a proper penalty-box predator? It is too early to say for certain but it is absolutely clear that he is taking up different positions, closer to the opponents’ goal, this season. Not only when the ball is on the left flank, but also when Arsenal are attacking through midfield.”

Saka starts among the substitutes this evening, but will play his part towards the end of the game.

Lille are considering legal ⁠action after defender Tiago Santos suffered a serious knee injury following an “uncontrolled and dangerous” tackle in Saturday’s match ‌against Le Havre.

Santos, 24, suffered a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament and meniscal tear in his right knee and was carried off the pitch on a stretcher after being tackled by Le Havre midfielder Amir Richardson during the first half of Lille’s 1-0 victory.

The referee gave a foul for the tackle but did not issue Richardson with a caution.

Lille said the ‌tackle merited ‌a red card ⁠and that they had asked the league’s governing body (LFP) to refer the matter to its disciplinary committee. The club are also seeking an explanation of ⁠the video review process undertaken by match officials.

“LOSC is exploring all possible legal avenues and reserves the right to take any legal action necessary to obtain compensation for its losses,” the ​club said. “It will support Tiago in ‌any steps he decides to take to defend his rights.”

The artist Northbanksy has plumped for another Oasis-inspired dig at Manchester City, this time with Rui Pinto taking centre stage, the man whose leaked emails kicked off the Premier League investigation into City’s financial affairs.

A consequence of Piero Hincapie’s injury on Saturday (he hurt his ankle in a cool-down session after the game, embarrassingly) is that Myles Lewis-Skelly is seemingly now the backup left-back. Arsenal can’t trust Riccardo Calafiori’s body to play two games in a week and are clearly saving him for Premier League action on the weekend. Lewis-Skelly has been so impressive in midfield that it must be frustrating to change position now.

Bakwa is on loan from Nottingham Forest, while those at the Emirates with long memories will remember that Nabil Bentaleb played for Spurs. Only the knowledgeable shall boo.

Lille XI: Özer; Perraud, Alexsandro, Ngoy, Goffi; Bentaleb, André; Mukau, Haraldsson, Bakwa; Ueda

Subs: Gill, Srdanovic, Giroud, Sahraoui, Kjaergaard, Onal, Kouassi, Verdonk, Cossier, Perrin, Diaoune, Sajous

Bukayo Saka, Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard drop to the bench, so some rotation from Arteta with a weekend trip to Nottingham Forest in mind, a venue where Arsenal have drawn 0-0 on their last two visits.

Arsenal XI: Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Lewis-Skelly; Bruno, Rice; Madueke, Merino, Eze; Gyokeres

Subs: Meslier, Kepa, White, Mosquera, Salmon, O’Neill, Hashi, Saka, Odegaard, Havertz, Dowman

Will Olivier Giroud receive a warm welcome back to the Emirates Stadium? The Frenchman spent six years as an Arsenal player but burned a few bridges when he left the club for Chelsea, and then celebrated wildly when Chelsea beat Arsenal in the Europa League final of 2019. Now 40, Giroud has shown remarkable longevity and is unquestionably one of the best strikers of his generation. But can he hurt this formidable Arsenal defence? It’s a tough ask.

Olivier Giroud back at the Emirates ❤️ https://t.co/TPBgcNDsVW

Arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

As Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal’s players will wear black armbands.

A post shared by Sam Dean (@samjdean_tel)

After signing his new Arsenal contract last week, Mikel Arteta described May’s Champions League final defeat as “poison in his veins,” and last season’s campaign demonstrated the benefits of finishing top of the league phase.

Arsenal enjoyed home second legs all the way through to the final after winning eight from eight, and in a 50:50 draw they fell into a considerably kinder bracket.

Sometimes it can be hard to gauge the importance of these league-phase matches, but Arteta will strive for another perfect record to give Arsenal the best possible chance of going deep in the competition again.

Fixtures against Bayern Munich and Real Madrid are likely to determine whether Arsenal finish in the top two, but there is still a job to be done against Lille this evening.

Arsenal have played against 10 different French opponents in European competition but have never faced Lille, who are managed by Davide Ancelotti, son of five-time Champions League winner Carlo.

Lille sell their best players every summer. After finishing third in Ligue 1 last season they lost Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to Manchester City and Newcastle United for a combined £130m. They have claimed 10 points from their first five league games of the season and led Paris St-Germain 2-0 before being pegged back in stoppage time.

Leading the line for Lille is 40-year-old Olivier Giroud, who scored 105 Arsenal goals in 235 appearances between 2012 and 2018. After leaving the Emirates, Giroud went on to score against Arsenal for Chelsea in the 2019 Europa League final, but he can still expect a warm reception.

Arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.

#1360. Stephen Robinson will carry the can for Aberdeen's woeful run but when do Dave Cormack and Lutz Pfannenstiel start getting it in the neck?

Published: 10:58 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 11:14 EDT, 6 November 2026

Few places are quite as spicy as Pittodrie when the locals have swapped the rustle of sweetie papers for the scent of blood in the nostrils.

Derek McInnes has been there. As have Stephen Glass and Jim Goodwin and Jimmy Thelin and plenty of others.

Current manager Stephen Robinson has been having a heck of a time of late too. The injury list is getting bigger and bigger as the patience with him dries up and everything points to it reaching crisis point on Saturday evening if the Dons, toiling for numbers or not, can’t see off Hibernian at home.

A number of punters didn’t fancy the ex-St Mirren boss from the off. And let’s be frank, results haven’t been good enough since he came in the door in March.

The reality is that Hearts are now the third force in Scottish football after a few years of jousting with Aberdeen, but that doesn’t mean expectations don’t remain high at Pittodrie.

A top-four finish is vital there in the wake of last term’s bottom-half struggles and beating the likes of Hibs, a club in a mess of its own right now, can be taken as a fair yardstick of how likely that is to happen.

Aberdeen manager Stephen Robinson faces a must-win game against Hibernian this weekend

Robinson needs a win. Should he suffer a fifth loss in six outings, he’ll be running the gauntlet for sure.

That’s the name of the game, but there’s just a couple of things before they bring out the tar and feathers and plan the great procession down King Street.

Not so long ago, sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel was sitting around the dugout with interim Peter Leven. He was a big presence. Had plenty to say. What’s he up to these days?

Same goes for chairman Dave Cormack. He has chucked a load of money into his first loves, for sure, but he is seven years in charge now and it’s not exactly easy to figure out where the club is going with no new stadium, little mention nowadays about the ties with Atlanta United, the club in danger of ending in the bottom six again and the summer suggesting there maybe isn’t quite the same moolah bouncing around to go on transfer fees.

If it all goes belly-up against Hibs and Robinson cops it over another season looking destined for the doldrums, fair enough. But shouldn’t Cormack and Pfannenstiel be getting it in the neck too?

#1359. A win to transport Martin O'Neill back to Celtic's European glory days? No, Besiktas was a lesson in why he shouldn't be the manager at all

Published: 11:22 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 12:00 EDT, 6 November 2026

There are clearly a number of ways in which to reflect upon Celtic’s quite discombobulating back-from-the-dead victory over Besiktas in the Europa League on Thursday evening.

Martin O’Neill regarded it as a triumph of heart and spirit and soul that conjured up recollections of ‘the olden days’, when the likes of Juventus, Porto and Olympique Lyon turned up at Parkhead during his first stint in charge and were sent packing with their tails between their legs.

Benjamin Nygren viewed it as a well-earned win notable for the side fighting from start to finish. Callum Osmand, meanwhile, opted to paint it as some kind of masterclass in digging in, staying strong and getting your rewards.

Of course, there are some of us sober-minded sorts who opted not to travel through the looking-glass and saw it for what it was. A disgrace, really. A night in which O’Neill appeared to buy into the overriding view of his paymasters that Europe doesn’t really matter all that much – only to get away with an unfathomable team selection by chucking on a load of subs over the last half-an-hour and hoping for the best.

It was a night, for anyone watching the game remotely objectively, that simply added fuel to the theory that the Northern Irishman is a man out of time and no longer suitable as manager.

He made comments afterwards about the team playing some lovely stuff. Gee-whizz. The first hour – before he summoned Camilo Duran, Osmand and Colby Donovan from the substitutes bench – was absolutely mortifying for Celtic as a club.

Martin O'Neill got his team selection wrong against Besiktas and was lucky to come out on top

It was like the olden days all right. The days when Wayne Biggins was running around up front and punters were throwing Mars bars into the directors’ box.

It’s just fortunate that Besiktas fell into such a false sense of security that they set about turning it into a game of ‘passy’, an exercise in keep-ball, and forgot about what those big white sticks at either end of the park are for.

For long periods, Celtic struggled to get the ball off them. When they did gain possession, they didn’t have the faintest idea what to do with it.

Early in the second period, with the visitors a goal up, a text came through from a foreign contact with an extensive history in the game who was questioning the wisdom of tuning in. ‘Really embarrassing’ was how he described it.

It was all that. And the madness and mayhem of the last 28 minutes or so shouldn’t be used to disguise it.

Celtic supporters paid good money for those Europa League packages and tickets. They need a better explanation than the one O’Neill gave in the aftermath for why they turned up for a make-or-break fixture and ended up watching the stiffs. They should claim a refund for the first 60 minutes.

The 3-2 victory, earned against all odds and much logic, showed precisely what was at stake. Celtic, thanks to Duran’s 87th-minute winner, are just a point off the top 24, which guarantees a spot in the play-offs. They’re also just four points off eighth and the automatic entry into the last 16 that brings.

There was absolutely everything to play for on Thursday. And that begs the painfully obvious question of why O’Neill picked the team he picked.

He says it was all intentional. That fresh legs were needed in the side. That the plan was always to utilise the substitutes the way he did. And the band played believe it if you like.

Camilo Duran is hailed by his team-mates but why he started on the bench remains a mystery

All the Dilly Daydreams buying into this stuff about it being a night for the ages and some sort of example of everything good about Celtic need to give their heads a wobble. This simply reeked of giving a home league game against Kilmarnock on Sunday priority over a big night under the lights.

The Parkhead side are in the state they are in because they have let their standards slip to a ridiculous degree. They have meekly accepted becoming a laughing stock in Europe, a punchbag for the LASKs and the Maribors and the Kairat Almatys.

Given O’Neill’s insistence that UEFA competition should be a major focus, it is crazy that he went into a game of this magnitude with Jordan Lotomba making his first start at right-back, 35-year-old James Forrest reappearing on the right flank for just his second start of the season and Sebastian Tounekti, a bloke that even the dogs in the street know is not cut out for this, on the left.

Lotomba had a mare, giving away the stupid penalty that led to Besiktas’ opener with a stupid tackle. Forrest did produce the team’s first shot on target on 50 minutes but was almost as ineffective as Tounekti. When all three departed the scene on 61 minutes, it wasn’t a moment too soon.

Surely the lightly raced Osmand, terrific after coming on, should have kept his place on the left. On the other side of the pitch, it’s hard to figure what is going on with £9million man Haissem Hassan. If he can’t get in the starting line-up ahead of the ageing Forrest, there’s a problem.

Right now, he’s starting to look a monumental waste of money that O’Neill doesn’t fancy. Indeed, the £20million or so committed to him and Kasper Hogh is starting to look like the most reckless example of silly spending since Edinburgh decided it needed to bring back the tram system.

Hogh should never have started. Duran should have been playing through the centre all day long and hammered that home when moving there after the Dane had been taken off and scoring twice.

Big Kasper is just a jigsaw piece in the wrong box here. A pineapple Danish in a bag of cinnamon swirls. Someone, somewhere will get some enjoyment from him through time, but it doesn’t look like it’s going to be Celtic.

O'Neill's relief at gaining a much-needed win was clear as he embraced assistant Maloney

That’s 15 games without a goal now. People can talk all they like about how O’Neill is not playing to his strengths, but an £11million international player needs to be able to adapt better than this. He was honking on Thursday. Again.

He just looks bereft of confidence, but wouldn’t it have been better to shove him in at home against Killie at the weekend in the hope he can get back on the goal trail rather than pitch him into a big European game and watch him slide ever further into the mire?

Lord knows. With every passing week, the mess the transfer window ended up being comes into sharper focus. Sam Johnstone doesn’t convince in goal and certainly didn’t convince against Besiktas.

It’s hard to know who should play between him and Viljami Sinisalo. Maybe both. A bit like Rab Douglas and Magnus Hedman all over again.

Still, it was good to see Landon Emenalo, Shim Mheuka and £3million Joel van den Berg get an outing in the KDM Evolution Trophy in Dingwall on Tuesday – and end up on the wrong end of a 2-0 hosing from League One Ross County, who had 22 shots on goal and rattled the woodwork more than once.

Yes, there are many things that can be said about the last couple of days at the champions. And lots of things that an admittedly thrilling win against solid opposition can paper over.

One thing remains as clear as it was before Besiktas came to town, though. Under this board and this manager, Celtic are a confusing outfit going nowhere other than backwards.

#1358. A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Inspired by macroscopic weaving techniques1,2,3,4, molecular weaving, which interlaces molecular strands into ordered networks, has emerged as a powerful strategy for designing functional materials with emergent properties5,6. However, so far, molecular weaving has relied mainly on linear building blocks and biaxial structures. Higher-order weaving (≥3 axes) of nonlinear building blocks is expected to produce intriguing architectures and bring new and unforeseen functions to the resulting materials; however, their construction and property investigation remain underexplored. Here we report a two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven polymer network constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into the woven structure through dative B–N polymerization. The resulting material not only exhibits unique topological chirality and robust mechanical properties but it also serves as a porous material that permits the separation of representative aromatic/aliphatic compounds. This functional utility highlights how higher-order triaxial woven topologies can provide unique advantages in terms of regulating material properties and introduces an extra topological dimension for the construction of functional materials.

#1357. Liverpool face Jeremie Frimpong transfer question as Saudi Pro League move emerges

Jeremie Frimpong’s Liverpool future has suddenly become uncertain, with the Netherlands international reportedly open to a move to Saudi Arabia just 18 months after arriving at Anfield.

The 25-year-old joined Liverpool from Bayer Leverkusen for around £29.5million in 2025, but injuries and competition at right-back have prevented him from becoming an undisputed starter.

That has now led to surprising speculation that his stay on Merseyside could be cut short.

According to WinWin, as reported by GOAL, intermediaries have offered Frimpong to Saudi Pro League giants Al-Hilal ahead of the January transfer window.

The report claims Frimpong would be open to discussing a move to Saudi Arabia, potentially giving him the opportunity to start again after an inconsistent spell in England.

However, there is currently no suggestion that Liverpool and Al-Hilal have entered formal negotiations.

Frimpong is receptive to a January departure, with intermediaries approaching Al-Hilal on his behalf. Liverpool could look for another right-back if he leaves, particularly with Frimpong struggling to consistently establish himself.

The biggest twist is that Al-Hilal may not actually want Frimpong.

A source close to the Saudi club told Kooora that Frimpong is not currently among their transfer priorities, with manager Simone Inzaghi instead focused on strengthening at centre-back and in midfield.

That makes this situation worth treating cautiously. Being offered to a club is very different from that club actively pursuing a transfer.

Liverpool also have little reason to force an exit. Frimpong remains contracted until 2030 and still offers elite pace and attacking quality when fit. His recent injury problems have disrupted his rhythm, but selling after only 18 months could prove premature.

There is clearly a debate to be had over whether Frimpong fits Liverpool’s long-term defensive plans.

However, unless Al-Hilal or another club make a significant offer, giving him more time to prove himself appears the more sensible approach.

#1356. Inside Mohamed Salah's new life after his Liverpool fall-out: LEWIS STEELE visits Turkey's 30th biggest city, where the Egyptian King hikes, drinks salted yoghurt - and still gets hero worship

Published: 07:03 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 12:12 EDT, 6 November 2026

It started just minutes after touchdown in Turkey.

In a taxi journey across Istanbul's intercontinental bridge to Fenerbahce's stadium, the driver took a break from lighting up a cigarette or shouting profanities at other road users. He turned, looked me in the eye, and asked: 'You know Mohamed Salah?'

Two and a half hours after fighting through mind-blowing traffic (think your gridlocked motorway at 5pm multiplied by 100), on arrival at Liverpool's press conference, one gentleman did not even exchange pleasantries. He shoved a selfie stick in my face and asked about Salah.

And these two encounters were 650 miles away from where the Egyptian player now plies his trade. This fandom was only a starter when compared to the main course of Salahmania that greeted us upon arrival in the port city of Trabzon, to the east of Turkey on the coast of the Black Sea.

Here, his face and name were everywhere you looked. 'You come for Salah?' enquired the hotel receptionist. Upon hearing that was indeed the purpose of the visit, he upgraded the room to a superior suite overlooking the ocean. Result.

The streets of this city, which feels a world apart from the bustling metropolis of Istanbul, never mind Liverpool, are packed with antique dealers, and markets selling two-foot-long fish for less than £1 and the local delicacy of hamsi (anchovy to you and me).

Mohamed Salah can relax in Trabzon and has taken multiple hiking trips in the highlands (Source: Instagram/Mohamed Salah)

Fans have now taken to posing at the same spots Salah appeared at - such is their hero worship

Everywhere you turned, there was a nod to Salah. His name was heard in conversations as the melodic call to prayer rang out from the nearby Hagia Sophia mosque, his picture seemed to be hung from every building and his name was on the back of every shirt being sported in town.

Shops were selling mugs, scarves, plates, masks and even cigarette lighters shaped like Salah.

At the futuristic waterfront stadium known as Papara Park, Salahmania continued - with punters putting on impromptu barbecues and DJ sets from beside their cars similar to tailgates in American sports. Everyone in this city was dancing to the beat of the Egyptian King.

Fans, many in Trabzonspor-coloured jester hats with bells on, glowed about Salah. Most do not speak a word of English in this city not far from the Armenian and Georgian border. But those who could summed up the mood.

'We love him, he is going to make us champions,' said one.

Another told us: 'People across the country now support Trabzonspor and people come from other countries, people want us to win just because of Mohamed Salah.'

Trabzonspor supporters told Daily Mail Sport: 'We love him, he is going to make us champions'

Everywhere you turned there was a nod to Salah in his new club's kit

There were plenty of children in the crowd, and more women than expected. Some had come from afar to see him, others could not believe that Salah had chosen their team and hometown.

So, why Trabzon? Why did Salah choose this project in Turkey's 30th biggest city? Why not one of the three Istanbul giants – Fenerbahce, Galatasaray or Besiktas – who have won 28, 27 and 21 Turkish titles respectively, compared to Trabzonspor's seven, including only one since 1984.

The answers are obvious, according to sources. Salah, now 34, wanted a place where he could enjoy his football without the intense scrutiny. Every word and facial expression would generate days of news coverage in Liverpool or Istanbul or another one of Europe's giant cities.

On the outskirts of Trabzon, Salah can relax, hiking up to a group of boulders in Yayla. Even there, he's worshipped, though. Trabzonspor fans flock there to pose for photographs on the same rock where he sat for a photo posted on his Instagram.

Salah's family are settled, he is becoming obsessed with chess and he has started drinking the Turkish salted-yoghurt drink ayran each day.

On the pitch, there is a belief Trabzonspor can beat the big three and end Galatasaray's four-year grip on the title.

The team also stars former Liverpool midfielder Fabinho and ex-Manchester United goalkeeper Andre Onana, while Jerome Boateng, once a stalwart at Bayern Munich, is assistant manager. Boss Thomas Reis was poached from Ludogorets and has lost just once since his arrival.

Salah is settled with his family and faces less scrutiny than in Istanbul or Liverpool (Source: Instagram/Mohamed Salah)

Salah has scored 10 goals and assisted five more in his 15 games in Turkey so far

The highlight so far came on September 19, when Salah scored a hat-trick in a 4-0 thumping of Galatasaray. Trabzonspor have won seven league games in a row and will aim to go deep in the Conference League despite Thursday's undeserved 1-0 defeat to Freiburg.

Salah has scored 10 goals and assisted in five more in his 15 games in Turkey.

'Everyone wants to work with a star the size of Mohamed Salah,' striker Paul Onuachu, once of Southampton, told us after that game. 'He is a top guy and a world star.

'He adds so much to us and helps all of us, thanks to his experience and quality, and he contributes positively to the development of our team.

'I am grateful for him. It is a blessing to play with him.'

Salah did not have the rub of the green in the clash with the German side, who were Europa League finalists last year. But a trip to Papara Park underlined an answer to those wondering just why he picked Trabzon and not any of his other mega-money offers.

A man wearing Trabzonspor's claret and light blue colours shows off his support for Salah

A trip to Papara Park underlined an answer to those wondering just why he picked Trabzon

He had approaches from America, and the Saudi Arabian federation tried to sign him right until the day he jetted into Trabzon - where he was greeted by 35,000 fans with fireworks and flares. Besiktas held advanced talks with Salah's agent Ramy Abbas.

But Trabzonspor won the race and Salah is playing with a smile again, even though that face pulled a bit of a grimace when he spotted a familiar face or two from the English press pack waiting for him after the game.

His laugh faded into an expression that said: 'I thought I got rid of you lot pestering me!'

That face confirmed his reason for joining Trabzonspor: Salah is out of the spotlight – certainly while still in with a chance to win trophies and maintain a good level of football until next summer's Africa Cup of Nations.

After a public fall-out with Liverpool that saw the final year of his contract ripped up and him accuse the Anfield club of 'throwing him under the bus', it feels like Salah is feeling at home and happy again.

It's not difficult to turn down the multiple opportunities to buy Salah-branded magnets or shirts or teddies or socks or lighters as we bid farewell to Trabzon, but it is hard to escape the conclusion that the feeling of love is mutual in this football-mad city.

#1355. Carrick’s United are in crisis and now spotlight is on Wilcox

Michael Carrick had urged his Manchester United players to come out and fight. But nobody could have imagined quite how Lisandro Martínez would interpret that message.

By the end of an extraordinary evening in Madrid, where United went 1-0 down inside a minute and never recovered against Atlético Madrid, Martínez had blown the lid off any pretence of all being well at the club as he launched a lacerating assault on the club’s executives.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

ATLETICO ARE AHEAD IN JUST 53 SECONDS! ⚡️ A nightmare start for United at the Metropolitano Stadium 😬 https://t.co/TdOwoXxopn

They certainly know how to make life difficult for themselves. Leny Yoro’s 74th-minute red card pretty much ended hopes of them taking something from the game.

Ademola Lookman scored Atlético’s second soon after and Carrick was staring at another defeat. And so they now move on to a big game at Leeds on Sunday. This was not the result Carrick would have wanted – and that is before what happened off the pitch.

Ademola Lookman PUNISHES a 10-man Man United 💥 https://t.co/GHKYIHGhNC

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

On the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

Martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring issues to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

Having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the company man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

It now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

That Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

United cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

[The performance] was a little bit mixed. It’s a tough enough place to come and the start we had put us in a difficult situation. I thought we grew into the game, had four big chances and [score one or more] and the game looks really different. They were really good chances.

And then the red card which I thought was a really poor one. It’s difficult after that. Disappointed that with the chances we had we didn’t [get] more [out of the game].

I haven’t seen [Martinez’s interview]. After a game like this you come here to try and get something from the game and you are disappointed and can be a little bit emotional. I have not seen it so I don’t think it is the right time for me to comment on it.

I fully know we all care and show that in different ways but now is the time to be together and work through. We have a big game on Sunday.

[What do you make of Lisandro’s comments?] I have no comment about that.

The only thing that’s going to get us back into it is to get a few wins.

It is very hard to say after a defeat that there are positives. We just have to work hard to keep working and keep trusting in our structure.

We have to keep working, keep trusting each other and be together on this.

I always wanted to be outspoken as a player but I think he’s gone too far. You can clearly see he cares and wants the club to invest more in new players but his performances have not been good enough. In some ways he’s right, the club needs to invest more. It looks like a bit of an agenda because it wasn’t a poor performance.

[How do you sum up the performance?] Really poor, Really poor. I have to control myself a lot. Sometimes it’s a mirror of the reflection of how our club is. We had a fantastic season last season but in order to compete we needed to buy more players. Many teams buy many players and Atletico Madrid did. They have an amazing team and deserved to win today.

I expected more. [Are you saying you expected more investment in the squad this summer?] Yes 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director. I have to be honest. As players we have to do more but it is important to make a strong squad to be ready for for this kind of night.

In general, in general [should you have invested more in defence and attack given all the midfielders]. Last season we made a strong base to build an amazing team. It’s annoying and disappointing coming here and trying to get a result.

I don’t think so [was the manager backed?] He does his best. You can’t [live on] what you did last season. Every season is different. You can’t stay with what you did last season. The teams knows how you play, they know every detail, if you don’t change next season is a big problem.

It’s changing, changing, changing the manager [after a poor run]. But what about other areas? I can’t say more.

Tonight is it easy to say the coach, easy to say the players [are at fault]. But we have to look at other areas.

So far this season there have been more times when the performances have been worse than the results. This was the other way round but there is a sizeable quality gap between Carrick’s squad and the company they are keeping. They can point to a soft red card but they still shot themselves in the foot with their doziness in the first minute and squandering the good chances they created.

Maguire strays offside when Mount, from the short corner, tries to pick him out at the back post.

Amad, now on the right, tries to dribble past Grimaldo who wins the ball off him but Atletico give it straight back. Man Utd work it into the box for Zirkzee to cushion and then dither so long over a shot he has to lay it off to Cunha who hits it straight at the keeper with two-thirds of the goal vacant. Oblak turns it wide.

Five minutes of stoppage time are signalled.

Alan Shearer says there has been improvement tonight since Saturday. “They have stuck together and have not been outrun.” This is a very low bar but OK. He goes on to say that the glaring weakness is not attitude but a lack of finishing quality.

And Le Normand is booked within seconds of his introduction for a tug of the shirt.

Dalot lofts a deep cross way beyond Zirkzee. I think Dalot encompasses Man Utd’s recruitment over the past eight years or so in that it’s hard to see any progression or improvement since the day they signed him. Maybe he always had a low ceiling. But where on earth is the coaching?

Manchester United have had their chances but they have lacked an elite or even merely decent finisher.

Atletico 2 Man Utd 0 (Lookman)  The three men were not enough and were carved apart by one pass from the left, from Grimaldo I think to David who opened his body to fire a shot towards the bottom right. Lammens dives to save but Lookman is Johnny on the spot to beat Dalot to the rebound and score.

Carrick now has three at the back after the sending off.

He places his hand on his shoulder and let it creep down on to Lookman’s chest as the former Everton winger tried to run clear from 40 yards.

The referee is sent to the screen to look again at Yoro’s contact on Lookman, the hand on the shoulder. Was it DOGSO, denial of a goalscoring opportunity. It was very weak.

Fernandes plays the corner to Amad standing to the left of the D, who rolls it halfway back and the captain wraps his foot around a blistering shot that thumps into the crossbar.

Cute pass from Heaven sends Amad down the left but still no target for him to find and he has to settle for a corner.

Mount wins the ball off Baena, passes out to Dalot on the right and he squares it to Bruno Fernandes. The captain opens his foot to shoot and the ball deflects off Zirkzee, killing its power. Oblak flops forward to gather.

Amad is on the left, Mbeumo to the right and Zirkzee down the middle with Fernandes tucked behind.

After Baena shoots at Lammens, Man Utd make a triple substitution:

Amad → RashfordMount → BalebaZirkzee → Tielemans.

Cross from the right. Bruno whips it around the left-back but Mbeumo, not really a centre-forward, held his line rather than running across Romero’s shoulder and that allows the former Spurs captain to get there first. Bruno signals his frustration.

Pubill goes to right-back and Llorente moves into midfield.

Baena cuts in off the left to shoot with his right, trying to curl it into the top right but the ball will not bend to his will and ends up being far to straight. He was looking for a banana bend and ended up with a cucumber.

Manchester United carve Atletico open with a simple long, left to right diagonal pass that Romero misjudges. Fernandes leaps to try to hook it on the volley over Oblak but instead steers it wide of the left post.

Terrific pass from Barrios picks out Alvarez on the left of the box and he thumps his shot into the post. Lammens, who dived to try to stop it, is stranded but Martinez is there to scramble the ball behind as it rebounded into the six-yard box.

Rashford slips Tielemans down the left and he stands up a cross that Oblan can pick out of the sky unmolested. Might be worth a gamble if they had Sesko to bring on.

Baena arrows a long cross straight at Lammens.

Good work from Baleba to win the ball off Barrios as the arrowhead of a three-man press but his chip down the left finds Rashford offside.

A foul on Fernandes is followed 40 seconds later by Rashford being penalised for trying to get past Simeone by holding his shoulder.

Yoro pushes high into the press and dispossesses Grimaldo and squares it to Bruno Fernandes. He clips a pass towards the penalty spot but too far from Mbeumo. Fernandes is patently unfit. I know he’s the captain/talisman but he is not very effective tonight.

No doubt Manchester United have improved and created a couple of chances for Mbeumo and one for Rashford. Baleba should really have buried that free back-post header from the corner, too. And that second Atletico ‘goal’ being disallowed was a real tonic on the stroke of half-time. Kudos fro not crumbling. But I wouldn’t be surprised if Baena, Alvarez and Lee carved them open again.

Tielemans is penalised for a foul on Cardoso who has no time to do anything with the free-kick in his own half.

No goal! He gained an advantage and the referee chalks it off.

Atletico 2 Man Utd 0 (Jonny Cardoso)  VAR check for handball.

Alvarez picks up his head and spanks a right-foot shot from 25 yards over the bar.

This feels a big moment for Carrick and United’s players to answer some of their critics. They have been getting battered from all sides in the last couple of days. Nicky Butt suggested on his podcast that Carrick told him before he got the United job that management “not for me” and “my head’s all over the shop” and that United was the only job he would take. At the very least, those comments are unhelpful and they are thought to have been dimly received internally.

Jamie Carragher offered a lacerating analysis of United’s performance against Spurs on Saturday on Sky Sports on Monday night and suggested things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved if there is not marked improvement. Steven Gerrard questioned why United opted to invest £50m of their summer budget in Andrey Santos, an unused substitute in the last three league games, insisted the back four was not good enough and questioned the work ethic.

And it was interesting to see Carrick alongside his mate Wayne Rooney just now pitchside. Rooney told the Stick to United podcast that captain Bruno Fernandes looks “fed up” and ready to explode at any moment.

It would have been pretty unthinkable for Carrick not to run with a three-man midfield here, not just because of the wide open spaces opponents have exploited this season but when you look at the back line United are fielding. Dalot at left back, two youngsters in Lenny Yoro and Ayden Heaven and a horribly out of form Lisandro Maríinez.

Nor has Senne Lammens looked convincing this term. Matheus Cunha has been dropped – not before time – and I expect to see Fernandes playing off the right. There’s going to a big onus on Rashford on the left. I’m not sure if he is fully fit but he’s going to be important.

It’s fantastic. It’s where we want to be, these games, these competitions. It’s as tough a place as you can come to. They’ve got a really good history in this competition and it’s where we want to come to challenge and test ourselves. We have put ourselves in this position, got a good start at home and now this is our first away game.

We want a reaction, of course. A positive reaction [to Saturday’s poor performance]. It hasn’t gone how we wanted, how we expected so far but it’s been fine margins in some of those games. It can go both ways but the reality is where we are at now.

It’s a fresh night and we’ve got to adapt, we’ve got to adjust in a positive way.

We want a little more control in the game [with three central midfielders]. At times we have been too open. We wanted to make a difference in that way. We’ve made other changes, certain spaces, certain positions.

To be honest it’s not really a big change of shape, personnel maybe but a lot of it is similar. We want more control, a little bit without the ball and a lot more with it. We’re happy with the way we set up.

Look at the last three goals we’ve conceded. They’re a mixed bag, simple goals you can something about. We need to defend better as a whole team .

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

The one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.

Liverpool are reportedly keeping a close watch on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki as they begin planning for life beyond Alisson Becker.

The Japan international has impressed since moving to Villa Park in the summer and is already attracting attention from several of Europe’s biggest clubs.

Liverpool’s interest is particularly significant because Alisson is in the final year of his contract, leaving the Reds with an important decision to make over one of the most influential players of their recent era.

According to TEAMtalk, Liverpool have checked on Suzuki while assessing their long-term goalkeeping options.

The 24-year-old joined Aston Villa for around £30million in the summer and has quickly impressed with his shot-stopping, distribution and ability to play as a modern sweeper-keeper. Real Madrid, Paris Saint-Germain, Arsenal, Manchester City and Tottenham are also monitoring him.

Villa, however, are under no pressure to sell. Suzuki signed a five-year contract and is considered a major part of their future, with TEAMtalk suggesting he could eventually command a world-record fee for a goalkeeper.

A CaughtOffside report also confirms Liverpool’s interest and notes that Suzuki is being viewed as a potential long-term successor to Alisson.

Liverpool would be wise to explore their options now rather than wait until Alisson actually leaves.

Manager Andoni Iraola admitted this week that he does not know whether the Brazilian will sign another contract, although discussions are taking place behind the scenes.

Alisson’s current deal expires next summer after Liverpool activated a one-year extension earlier in 2026.

Liverpool already have Giorgi Mamardashvili and highly-rated youngster Lucca Brughmans in their plans, but TEAMtalk reports that Mamardashvili is not currently viewed as Alisson’s definitive long-term replacement.

That makes Suzuki an understandable target. He is young, already Premier League-tested and possesses the distribution required in Iraola’s system.

The difficulty will be price. Villa have little reason to sell, and Liverpool could face competition from several elite clubs.

Still, if Alisson does depart in 2027, Suzuki looks like exactly the type of goalkeeper Liverpool should be considering.

#1353. Exiled Jack Grealish RETURNS to Everton training after being dropped following boozy nights at pubs and karaoke: Ex-England star could be back in team after international break

Published: 12:34 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 14:16 EDT, 6 November 2026

Jack Grealish will return to Everton training after being dropped and exiled by David Moyes.

The 31-year-old was axed for back-to-back matches against Newcastle following a 'breach of club discipline' and is not part of the Toffees' matchday squad for the third game on the spin when they host Coventry tonight.

Grealish, who has made seven appearances since re-joining Everton for a second season-long loan spell from Man City in the summer, had been banished since failing to show up for a training session on Monday last week. It is understood staff struggled to make contact with the winger.

Grealish will now be reintegrated on a tailored training programme to regain match fitness and could be included in first-team sessions during the international break from next week.

Grealish had made four successive starts before he missed Everton's 2-0 defeat by Arsenal on October 24 due to illness.

Grealish was reported to have had back-to-back nights out prior to the Toffees' defeat in north London.

Jack Grealish, previously pictured out with a friend, was exiled by Everton but is now set to return to training with the team

David Moyes could start Grealish against Brentford after the international break

The three-time Premier League winner attended the Pride of Britain awards at the Grosvenor House hotel in London on October 19 where he presented the Child of Courage award to 12-year-old Zac Howells.

He is then reported to have finished the night of celebration off at Bam Karaoke Box, a karaoke hotspot in Victoria, central London.

According to the Sun, he stayed up until the early hours of the morning singing with his friends and enjoying the drinks on offer.

The next day, Grealish is believed to have returned to Cheshire, where he and many of his footballer friends live, to meet team-mates Jordan Pickford and Tyler Dibling at The Mauldeth pub in Wilmslow.

The trio, joined by Grealish's former City team-mate and captain Kyle Walker, where they watched Paris Saint-Germain's thrilling Champions League victory over Barcelona. A witness claimed to the Sun that they enjoyed a few drinks.

Moyes had been coy on the situation when asked about it on Thursday. He said: 'You probably know I'm not going to give any details, it is a club decision and I support that decision (for him to be punished). It is something I don't want to speak too much about.

'The one thing about Everton is that we have got really good values behind it. All the players stand up to the values and accept the values, on the pitch and off the pitch. From that point of view, I think the players did a brilliant job.'

Without Grealish once again, Everton are seeking to secure a third win in a row when they come up against former Toffees boss Frank Lampard and his Coventry team.

Grealish is reported to have gone on consecutive nights out after attending the Pride of Britain Awards on October 19

After the Coventry clash, Everton are next in Premier League action at Gtech Community Stadium against Brentford on November 23.

Grealish will be targeting a return in that fixture and hope he can begin to rebuild his relationship with Moyes over the next three weeks.

He has played for England 39 times and turned out for Everton on 22 occasions, scoring twice and providing six assists, with a nasty foot injury cut short his campaign last term.

There was no grand gesture as Bradley Barcola walked back to the bench, just a high-five from Andoni Iraola and some of Liverpool’s coaching staff.

It was a similar situation as he left the stadium. Hood up, jacket zipped, baseball cap pulled on tightly, he politely turned down all requests to talk in English. “Not good enough,” he said with a smile, but that was the only thing that had not been up to standard.

The giveaway here was what he held in his right hand – the match ball. On it were the signatures of Liverpool’s squad, congratulating him on a momentous performance that had arrived right on cue.

If you are going end a barren spell, you do not want to just turn on the taps but burst the dam, and that is precisely what Barcola did on a wild night in Austria. He needed one goal to get his Liverpool career up and running, he ended up scoring three.

Iraola had said he was not concerned about Barcola’s numbers when Liverpool arrived in Linz, even if no goals and no assists since his £123m move from Paris St-Germain had caused debate, but those numbers look infinitely better now after his first senior hat-trick.

“He was always one-on-one, certainly in behind and he helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am happy for both of them, yes. For their confidence for sure, it’s very good. I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. It’s going to be very good for them.”

The home team moving the ball around with some confidence, but they look so vulnerable to Liverpool’s counter-attacks whenever they lose possession.

That LASK attack carried more punch though: there was an important defensive touch from Nyoni, before Lang fires just wide of the post at the edge of the box.

How many more goals will Liverpool add to their tally in the second half?

Flecker replaces Jorgensen. Iraola has decided against making any subs.

19 - Liverpool have recorded the most shots by an away team on record in the first half of a UEFA Champions League away match (since 2003-04). Volume. https://t.co/AFlsqZlKFh

Liverpool well on their way to consecutive wins in the Champions League league phase, and the big positive is the threat offered by Barcola, Wirtz as well as Ngumoha. Barcola and Wirtz also offered signs of a promising partnership. The gulf in class is stark, and Iraola can now make changes with Brentford in mind.

Wirtz looking a far more confident player, not that this is the most exacting test, and he tests the goalkeeper with a curling shot towards the far corner. There will be just one minute of added time to play.

Liverpool’s wingers Barcola and Ngumoha have just been far to sharp for their markers, LASK cannot cope with the pace on offer. The home team keep pushing numbers forward which could be a dangerous straregy.

That’s a very nifty assist from Florian Wirtz, played through legs into Barcola’s feet in the box, and the French winger’s touch teed him up for a left-footed finish across the goalkeeper. Game over, which was already the case.

What a difference a goal makes. Barcola’s touches and feints and skills are getting a full airing now and rightly so. He looks like he is relaxing and he should be aiming to score himself a hat-trick. Liverpool are miles clear of this team.

Writing Partnership building... 👀 Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola link up for Liverpool's third 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/AffQ8kSy2C

This game is a non-contest. Gravenberch lines up another shot from the edge of the box, before Barcola shows some quick feet in the box and his side-footed attempt loops over. The question for Iraola is the extent to which these performances and chances created will translate to Premier League standard.

Ryan Gravenberch so unlucky not to score with a shot across Jungwirth, which struck the inside of the far post and bounced away to safety, before a Wirtz shot deflects behind. Liverpool waltzing through the LASK defence with ease now.

Lewis Koumas thought he had scored a third for Liverpool, but the flag was raised for offside. He was a yard or two off, but it was still a very accomplished finish.

Liverpool just need a goal or two from Wirtz now and the night would be complete. LASK actually made a confident start in the first 20 minutes but conceding from a corner has deflated them.

Barcola is the scorer, but the initial danger was instigated by Ngumoha, dribbling around the outside of the LASK defence and into the box where he is tackled. The ball breaks free to Koumas, and he sets it back for Barcola to find the far corner. Liverpool now in command.

The goals have been coming from Liverpool and, really, it should be a night for them to plunder a hatful. LASK have loud supporters and the atmosphere being created is typically of one of these smaller European stadiums but Liverpool are miles better than LASK and should rip them apart. Bradley Barcola looked like a weight had been lifted as he got his first goal and you would now like to see him get a couple more – it’s certainly possible for him to do so.

Bradley Barcola gets off the mark for Liverpool with an instinctive finish 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/5K7YBB7UyG

A Van Dijk-esque header you could say, and Liverpool have punished LASK’s jittery set-piece defending. Good delivery from Tsimikas, and Araujo rose highest around seven yards out to plant a header byone Jungwirth.

Araujo rises to score his first goal for Liverpool 🔴 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/W1C4iYd89m

Some harrying from Gravenberch is enough to win Liverpool another corner, their fifth of the game so far. The goalkeeper was shaky again, but the ball glances off a LASK head and out for another corner.

LASK are targetting Liverpool’s left flank with direct balls forward, and the big centre-forward Adeniran caused Jacquet all manner of problems near the touchline but his touch ran away from him in the box.

The another good Barcola run is found, but his shot is screwed just wide of the near post. Barcola and Wirtz certainly more involved so far.

Diligent defending from Jorgenson to halt the progress of Barcola after a burst into the penalty area from the left. From the Liverpool corner, LASK goalkeeper Jungwirth was uncertain but Araujo could not not get enough on the header.

There really is something incongruous about seeing Kostas Tsimikas wearing the Liverpool captain’s armband. He should never have been given it again after throwing it on the floor after a pre-season friendly in the United States when he, Curtis Jones and Dominik Szoboszlai bickered with each other. The reason Alisson doesn’t wear it is because if there is a decision that requires him to talk to the referee in the opposition area, he would be miles from his own goal and potentially vulnerable. Alisson is the real leader on this pitch for this team.

Liverpool starting to turn their screw now. First, Wirtz skipped through a couple of challenges and fired a low shot straight at the goalkeeper before Ngumoha, playing on the right, drops a shoulder and drives to the byline, standing up a dangerous cross.

Then Wirtz tries another dribble through the middle, but his shot is charged down.

Liverpool struggling to clear their lines from the corner, and Schopf scoops a shot over the bar from the edge of the area.

Nyoni then tries a difficult reverse pass back towards Barcola but overcooks it. Moments before, there was a nice touch from Barcola to bring down a switch of play.

Lewis Koumas looking dangerous again, peeling behind LASK’s defence and rounding the goalkeeper Jungwirth on the corner of the penalty area, but he was forced wide and had to settle for a corner which the goalkeeper claims.

Then LASK pour forward again after a cheap giveaway by Araujo, and the home team win a corner of their own. Lively enough start.

Tsimikas scrambling rather to deal with a cross towards Jorgensen, before Alisson puts Liverpool under pressure with a stray pass, and LASK have a corner. Taken short, and then stood up to the back post but Liverpool clear.

Kostas Tsimikas captains Liverpool tonight, not words I ever expected to type but it is a team short of experience. Liverpool enjoying all of the possession so far, LASK are defending in a 5-2-3 shape, so Liverpool’s full-backs should have some time and space. Gravenberch does well to win a foul in midfield.

The home team play in all red, so Liverpool are in their white away strip. It looks like there is some Liverpool support among the locals/neutrals in the home end.

LASK XI: Jungwirth, Jorgensen, Mbuyamba, Alemao, Andrade, Dibango, Danek, Bogarde, Schopf, Lang, Adeniran

Subs: Schutzenauer, Schillinger, Freckleton, Ljubicic, Kalajdzic, Verhaeghe, Elfadli, Flecker, Kane.

A young Liverpool team has been selected to face Linz – the third youngest, according to Opta, that the club have fielded in the Champions League – and Andoni Iraola is being mindful of players such as Virgil van Dijk and Alexis Mac Allister being overburdened ahead of Saturday’s trip to Brentford.

One novice who certainly deserves his starting spot is Trey Nyoni, the England Under-21 international has impressed in the opportunities he has been given so far this year. Watch out for his calmness on the ball and the efficiency with which he uses it.

He should get more chances in the next 10 days, as it is difficult to see Dominik Szoboszlai being ready at least until the home match against Brighton on Sunday week.

Asked about Liverpool’s youthful team, Iraola said: “For me Trey [Nyoni], [Lewis] Koumas and Rio [Ngumoha] are young players coming in from the academy but they are first team players.

“They are first team players because we trust them, and in our situation, where we have some injuries, and we come from playing three days ago. I think they can play well, and I hope they do well.”

24 - Liverpool's starting XI against LASK has an average age of 24 years and 186 days, their third-youngest ever for a UEFA Champions League game, older only than September 2001 v Borussia Dortmund (24y 136d) and December 2020 v Midtjylland (24y 26d). Knocks. https://t.co/4JeW73N87k

Iraola makes four changes from the defeat by City so in come Frimpong, Tsimikas, Nyoni and Ngumoha.

Liverpool XI: Alisson, Frimpong, Araujo, Jacquet, Tsimikas, Nyoni, Gravenberch, Wirtz, Barcola, Koumas, Ngumoha

Subs: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Van Dijk, Kerkez, Mac Allister, Munoz, Chambers, McConnell, Danns, Sonni-Lambie, Lucky

Our team to take on LASK ✊ #UCL https://t.co/8vObg7mgLF

It is early days for Bradley Barcola but is has been an underwhelming start to his Liverpool career. The winger was a rotational player at Paris St-Germain, as he is for France, so Liverpool spending £120m is a gamble on his raw athletic attributes and the hope that he pieces everything together.

As Dominic King writes in this piece: “Barcola had no control over the price that Richard Hughes, Liverpool’s former sporting director, brokered with Paris St-Germain for his release. But something he can control is public perception and, with no goals or assists so far, opinions are starting to form.”

Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

They travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

“You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

“Especially now we are playing four games in 10 days, it’s keeping all the legs, all the energy in the games.

LASK are currently third in the Austrian league, but booked their place in this season’s Champions League proper with a remarkable comeback from 4-0 down on aggregate against Celtic.

They have injury problems of their own to contend with George Bello and Moses Usor limping off in the weekend’s defeat by league leaders Rapid Wien and Ramiz Harakate tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in July.

They do play on a grass pitch at the Raiffeisen Arena though Kasper Schmeichel, the former Celtic goalkeeper who was working as a TV pundit for the game, was critical of the playing surface.

Manchester United are emerging as the Premier League club showing the strongest interest in Como centre-back Jacobo Ramón as they begin planning the next stage of their defensive rebuild.

The 21-year-old has enjoyed an outstanding rise under Cesc Fàbregas in Italy, establishing himself as one of Serie A’s most promising young defenders.

His performances have now earned him a first senior Spain call-up, while United, Chelsea and Liverpool are all monitoring his progress.

According to AS, Man United have been the most persistent English club in their pursuit of Ramón, although Chelsea and Liverpool are also keeping the defender on their radar. Read the AS report on Jacobo Ramón

Ramón is currently focused on Como and is not expected to leave during January, meaning any serious transfer battle is more likely to develop next summer.

The biggest complication for United is Real Madrid. Los Blancos retained 50 per cent of Ramón’s rights when selling him to Como and can reportedly bring him back for around €10million.

Madrid remain impressed by his progress and could eventually exercise that option before deciding whether he has a place in their first-team squad.

Fàbregas has previously made his admiration clear, describing Ramón as “a young player with a great future” when discussing the defender’s potential.

From a Man United perspective, the interest makes plenty of sense.

Ramón is young, physically imposing at 1.96m and comfortable building attacks from defence. He has also developed a goalscoring threat, contributing three goals and two assists for Como this season.

United have already seen his quality first-hand. Ramón scored during Como’s 4-1 Champions League victory over them in October, a performance that reportedly strengthened their interest.

United have increased their monitoring of the Spaniard as they assess potential defensive additions for 2027.

The difficulty is that United do not control the situation. Madrid’s inexpensive buy-back clause gives them a huge advantage, while Ramón is attracting interest from several major clubs.

Still, United should remain in the conversation. If they want to build a younger, more technically secure defence, Ramón fits that strategy extremely well.

#1349. Celtic's Europa League win over Besiktas a welcome boost ... but Mika Baur says belief has always been there

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 14:32 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 14:41 EDT, 6 November 2026

It's fair to say that the way in which Martin O’Neill got Celtic off the mark in the Europa League against Besiktas divided public opinion.

For many of those viewing a starting line-up including Jordan Lotomba, Seb Tounekti and James Forrest, the veteran lucked out.

The opposing take was that O’Neill executed a managerial masterclass. That the belated introductions of Callum Osmand, Camilo Duran and Colby Donovan constituted a textbook rope-a-dope approach.

Whatever the truth of the matter, and only O’Neill truly knows what it is, you could not possibly argue with the outcome.

Second best in the contest for an hour, Celtic improved markedly in the final 30 minutes and refused to accept a share of the spoils when it seemed destined to be their lot.

How you finish a match is, indeed, just as important as how you start it. And it helps, of course, when those who belatedly enter the fray bring not only goals but pace, panache and a positive attitude.

Midfielder Mika Baur has been a standout performer in an up-and-down season for Celtic

‘That’s what you want from the subs — to make an impact from the bench,’ said midfielder Mika Baur.

‘It says a lot for Camilo to accept the situation of starting on the bench. But to come on and make such an impact, producing in the big moments to score those two goals to win us the game was huge.

‘Ossie [Osmand] as well, he came on with a goal and assist. He won the ball as well and was working hard. I’m really glad for them.’

In every respect, Celtic needed a night like that. O’Neill walked off the team coach before the game knowing a loss would see him become the first manager in the club’s history to oversee five straight European defeats.

With the wider picture of just three wins in ten matches, the scatter gun had been trained on everyone at the club in recent days – the hierarchy, the players, the manager and his coaching staff.

‘The win was important after some tough weeks,’ Baur reflected. ‘But the belief and the way we work together as a team has always been good. There was never any problem with that because we always believed in ourselves.

‘We showed how we can leave our hearts on the field and put in a shift. It was important to get those three points and we deserved it.

‘Hopefully, we can go forward with the confidence from this game.’

Given the air of gloom which has hung over the club lately, the Turks’ opener, stemming from a ludicrous tackle by Lotomba, felt for all the world like an extension of so much which had gone before.

From the minute Osmand levelled with his first touch, however, the entire dynamic of the evening changed.

Celtic found something deep within themselves that just hadn’t been there up until that point. The positivity on the field was mirrored by the buoyant mood in the stands.

The introductions of Callum Osmand and Camilo Duran turned Thursday's clash on its head

‘The fans helped a lot. You could feel the energy,’ said Baur. ‘It was not just us players on the field who deserved the win — it was also everyone around the stadium and they brought the energy as well.

‘It’s an unbelievable feeling as a player to have everyone pushing you and being there for you. It gives you that last percentage of energy you need at the end.’

Technically impressive and tactically astute, Baur caught the eye on Thursday, just as he has done in most of his matches since moving to Glasgow from Paderborn for £4.5million in the summer.

Whatever criticisms can justifiably be made of the club’s recruitment across a number of years, the German has already justified the faith shown in him.

It’s easy to forget that he’s still only 22. The level of scrutiny he’s being subjected to in Glasgow is a new thing. So far, however, he’s shown up well.

‘Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t,’ he shrugged. ‘But I hope people understand that as a young player it can be tough to be comfortable in a new country, a new culture and new club.

‘I have felt good in my first few months but it is a bit of a rollercoaster. Playing in this unbelievable stadium in front of these fans — you feel the pressure with some of the games we have lost, but I am getting used to it.’

Having earned his first full cap in September after being called up by new Germany boss Jurgen Klopp, Baur has dropped back down to the Under-21s in the coming fortnight but takes only positives from his experience of the last international camp.

‘I can understand,’ he said. ‘There are so many unbelievable players in the squad, especially in my position.

‘We’re talking about guys from Bayern Munich and Borussia Dortmund. I just do my best and hopefully they can see I am developing and improving.

‘I’m still with the Under-21s for the games against Belgium and Croatia, so that will be good.

‘European matches like Thursday can only help and I have to hope they see. I’m still young but I’ll keep doing my best and we’ll see what happens next time.’
