#1348. Thomas Tuchel admits his relationship with Jude Bellingham is 'up and down' - but on the mend - as he reveals he's apologised to Kobbie Mainoo who is struggling at 'off a cliff' Man United

Published: 14:00 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 15:27 EDT, 6 November 2026

Thomas Tuchel says his rocky relationship with Jude Bellingham is on the mend after revealing he called his brother Jobe in to the England squad after some cajoling from the Real Madrid star.

Tuchel and Bellingham Snr have not always seen eye to eye during the German's time as England boss.

But Tuchel said today he hopes those days are behind him after he called 21-year-old Borussia Dortmund midfielder Jobe into this squad for next week's Nations League games against Croatia and Spain.

'It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course but we are in a good place,' said Tuchel.

'I love to be his coach. He's a top player, a very influential player and I think it goes both ways. If Jude was not feeling comfortable he would not perform on that level.

'In the moment you see he's happy to come into camp, he's happy with the role he has, he's fully invested and now to have the chance to have both of them is just the next step.

Thomas Tuchel has admitted he has an up and down relationship with Jude Bellingham

'I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach!'

With injury to Bournemouth's Alex Scott and Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly suspended for Thursday's Croatia game at Wembley, Tuchel sprung a surprise by elevating Jobe Bellingham from the Under 21s to the senior squad.

'Yeah Jude and I have spoken about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream to play with Jobe for England,' explained Tuchel.

'Jude was always saying: "Watch him, watch him he's good, he can make it". 'I would say: "Yeah we are watching him".

'I think he actually watched training very early in my reign. He came over and watched his brother train. We chatted and said it would be nice if one day he was with him.

'He was very kind and very polite and I'm glad to have him in camp. Everyone will compare them and he has to live with this.

Now Tuchel says he 'loves' to be Bellingham's coach after his brilliant World Cup campaign

Jude had a hand in brother Jobe being called up to the England squad for the first time

'They look similar, even in their movements, but they are very different players. Jobe is more defensive. I think they are also different characters, at least that's what I heard.

'He couldn't stop smiling when I called to tell him the news. He has the same beautiful smile like Jude so it's nice to have him.'

Tuchel's squad for what he insists are two important games was once again full of messages and insights into this thinking.

There was no room for Cole Palmer and Kobbie Mainoo after both players withdrew from the October campo with injuries. There was also no call up once again for Manchester City's Phil Foden.

Asked about Palmer, fit and ready now and in decent form at Chelsea, Tuchel said: 'It's not personal and we will never assume that he is not desperate to come and play.

'But the competition is on. It's about the ones who walk the walk and come to camp.

'Someone more intelligent once said to me: 'You cannot not communicate. You cannot not send a message.'

'So yeah. A nomination is always a message, yes.'

Tuchel revealed that he almost picked Foden – who hasn't played for England since March – after an upturn in his form but had second thoughts when he saw him relegated back to the bench at the Etihad Stadium.

'He is close and he will always be close,' said Tuchel.

'There were glimpses of the Phil Foden that we would love to see. He had these two matches with four or five goal involvements and assists and being so clinical.

Cole Palmer continues to be left out by Tuchel - while Phil Foden was close to a recall

'I got excited and thought: "That's it, that's, he found his mojo, he is getting back there". Then he dropped again and played again from the bench.

'I'm in love with him as a player. What is not to love?

'If you see the boy train it's just the highest, highest quality.

'But we're talking about numbers in an England shirt which are not in proportion to his talent and to his potential.

'If we can align this and become a regular City starter and be decisive, I think he has to be always an option.

'It was very close and it's also close for Eberechi Eze to keep his place with us. He's not starting for Arsenal.

'But the advantage was maybe that Morgan Gibbs-White and Eberechi Eze come again into camp. The advantage was that they have been in camp last time.'

Thomas Tuchel has told how he apologised in front of the whole England squad to Kobbie Mainoo for not giving him a single minute during the summer's World Cup in America.

Mainoo cut a lost and frustrated figure during England's campaign after a succession of players were picked ahead of him in his central midfield position.

The Manchester United star has not made Tuchel's squad for the forthcoming Nations League games with Croatia and Spain after withdrawing from the last camp with injury.

Tuchel revealed: 'He was hugely disappointed from the World Cup, and deservedly so.

'I said it in front of the team, in front of the staff.

'I said: "Sorry that I didn't pick you, you did nothing wrong, that is on me".

'He was disappointed and I think it cost him a bit of confidence.

Tuchel has noted how Man United 'fell off a cliff' - causing issues for Kobbie Mainoo

'He was excellent in training and in the way he presented himself through the tournament.

'So he was never a problem, the way he carried himself.

'Then he pulled out of last camp. I was desperate to give him the minutes. Desperate to include him in this new start, in the Nations League.

'But he then missed an excellent camp and also entered a difficult, difficult spell for himself.

'He was injured then Man United fell off a cliff a little bit performance-wise. So this is why he suffers from that.'

Manchester United are increasingly expected to bring in a new striker during the January transfer window, with Benjamin Sesko’s injury exposing a clear lack of depth through the middle.

United chose not to prioritise another centre-forward during the summer, instead focusing resources on strengthening midfield. That decision is now being tested, with Sesko sidelined and Joshua Zirkzee struggling to convince Michael Carrick that he should lead the line.

Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha have both been used centrally, but neither is a natural No.9. As a result, the club’s January plans appear to be shifting towards a short-term solution rather than another major long-term investment.

According to The National, United are now likely to pursue a striker on loan when the January window opens.

The club are believed to be working within financial restrictions and do not want to commit a large fee to another centre-forward before the summer.

Sesko is still viewed as the long-term focal point of the attack, so a temporary deal would allow United to cover his absence without disrupting that plan.

United’s urgency has increased because Sesko is not expected back before the start of 2027, while Zirkzee continues to see limited action.

The Dutchman is not considered part of United’s long-term plans.

A loan deal makes plenty of sense for United.

They need someone capable of starting immediately, but spending heavily on another young striker could create a problem once Sesko returns. The priority should be experience, reliability and minimal adaptation time.

That explains the growing interest in Ivan Toney. CaughtOffside reported that United are exploring a loan move for the Al-Ahli striker, who has Premier League experience and could provide an immediate physical presence up front.

Jean-Philippe Mateta is another realistic option. The Crystal Palace striker remains firmly on United’s radar, helped by his proven Premier League record and expiring contract.

United’s summer decision to prioritise midfield was understandable, but the lack of a dependable back-up striker now looks costly.

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

When Manchester City endured their first major sanction over financial fair play in 2014, the biggest club accused alongside them that summer were Paris St-Germain, another Champions League arriviste who had been raised from mediocrity to the elite by some frantic spending from a Middle East fossil fuel dynasty.

Then, 12 years ago, both sides bitterly opposed the Uefa sanctions imposed on them – although they eventually agreed to the terms. Now, they face one another in Manchester with PSG aiming for a third consecutive Champions League title, and City fighting for their lives in the face of an overwhelming guilty verdict for nine years of Premier League rule-breaking.

Both clubs are transformed from the entities that their current owners acquired. While PSG now find themselves at the centre of the new order in European football, City are once again on the outside.

Whatever the outcome of this process, I won’t forget the connection and relationships I had here. It will never be erased.

Good evening, and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Manchester City and Paris St-Germain, champions in 2025 and 2026 and favourites to become only the fourth club, after Real Madrid (who have done it twice), Ajax and Bayern Munich to win a hat-trick of European Cups.

After Manchester City’s conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has said he would prefer not to cover City’s games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the issues addressed.

Having said that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don’t think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. I propose once the match starts to treat it as a match while not ignoring the context.

Right, let’s get stuck into the Gulf State sovereign wealth fund derby… sorry, imposible to resist.

#1345. Why are we conscious? Nature investigates the theories

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Amanda Heidt is a freelance journalist in southeast Utah.

Imaging can be used to measure the degree of variation and complexity across brain regions that correspond to conscious states.Credit: AJ Photo/Hop Americain/SPL

At first glance, human consciousness seems like the one thing we should never have to doubt. We know we are conscious because we experience the world in vivid detail: the small luxury of a piece of chocolate; a song imbued with sadness; or a childhood memory that takes us back to another place and time.

But for such a fundamental aspect of reality, what underlies consciousness — the experience of being aware of one’s own existence — has proved deceptively hard to pin down. Researchers and philosophers have spent centuries debating how and why physical processes in the brain result in the subjective, first-person experiences we all seem to have. This issue, known as the ‘hard problem’ of consciousness, continues to drive research today.

Scientists are still far from explaining how brain activity begets an entire inner world, but the field is making progress. The advances that researchers have made include the ability to reliably measure brain activity and connectedness and probe for signs of hidden awareness.

The emerging picture — based on insights from not just neuroscience, but also far-flung disciplines such as plant science, artificial intelligence and astrobiology — is not of consciousness as a single light that can be switched on, but as a coordinated condition that is potentially more widespread than previously thought. The rapid rise of AI, for example, has fuelled discussions over whether only humans can be conscious — and of whether a brain is even required for consciousness.

“People are often troubled by the fact that our understanding remains somewhat vague,” says Matthias Michel, a philosopher of cognitive science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. “However, it’s very important to note that definitions in the history of science come at the end of the scientific process, not at the beginning. I’d argue we’re now in the thick of it, which is an exciting place to be.”

There is no direct test for evaluating human consciousness, but researchers have made advances in establishing what are known as neural correlates of consciousness (NCCs). These criteria, which can be a single metric or a combination of events, identify the minimum neuronal mechanism required to kickstart a conscious experience. Specific neurons might need to fire, for example, and particular brain activity patterns could signify an internal experience. Below these thresholds, a person might move through life not fully conscious of their behaviour — zoning out while driving, for instance, only to snap back to attention moments later.

Some NCCs have been determined by studying people in states we don’t typically associate with consciousness, such as those who are asleep, anaesthetized or in a coma. According to Melanie Boly, a neurologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, this type of research is crucial to help separate true NCCs from activities that merely signify being awake and responsive to our surroundings.

“That’s been a big breakthrough, isolating the true features of consciousness, rather than simply measuring something that is associated with or a consequence of the conscious experience,” Boly says.

Is social media changing children’s brains? Here’s what the science says

Is social media changing children’s brains? Here’s what the science says

Through that work, scientists know that about one-quarter of individuals who present as medically unconscious are, in fact, experiencing a type of covert consciousness in which they continue to perceive the world around them. In a landmark 2024 study, a subset of 241 people who had been left seemingly unresponsive by brain injuries were asked to imagine themselves engaging in activities such as playing tennis or opening and closing their hand. Dozens of patients’ brains became active on imaging scans during these challenges — calling into question whether consciousness persists in otherwise-inert states1.

In recognition of this finding, researchers have moved away from thinking of consciousness as a binary experience towards an understanding that consciousness is a dynamic process that exists on a continuum. From these principles, it has been possible to develop metrics that test the underlying scientific assumptions about consciousness. One of the most promising of these is called the perturbational complexity index (PCI)2.

PCI evaluates a person’s level of consciousness by assessing how their brain responds to a brief magnetic pulse, as measured by electroencephalography (EEG), which traces the brain’s electrical activity using electrodes. In a conscious brain, the neural response usually spreads while remaining complex and distinct from one brain region to another — features referred to as integration and differentiation, respectively. During sleep or under anaesthesia, the response becomes simpler and more repetitive.

“PCI is considered to be a very accurate correlate of consciousness that can be useful in many research settings,” says Johan Frederik Storm, a neurophysiologist at the University of Oslo. Widespread clinical adoption has unfortunately been hampered by the fact that it’s a laborious metric to gather, he adds, “but even still, it is gaining traction”.

This growing understanding has led to the development of hypotheses that move beyond simply measuring aspects of consciousness towards a more foundational understanding of what it is. At present, there are more than 450 such theories, many of which share overlapping features even as they distinguish themselves by scale or focus. The two most popular are the global neuronal workspace theory (GNWT) and the integrated information theory (IIT).

The GNWT posits that most brain activity is restricted to specialized areas — visual regions process shapes and colours, for example, and language areas process words. Consciousness emerges when information becomes important enough to be broadcast across regions. A face whose representation remains inside the visual system might trigger a simple, unconscious reaction, but a face that triggers regions across the brain, collectively known as the global workspace, can be used by many systems to build a conscious experience.

The IIT tries to answer a different question: what is experience like? When we view the world or recall a memory, we experience a cohesive scene, not separate elements of colour, sound and touch. The IIT argues that consciousness depends on how strongly the parts of a system affect one another while still remaining distinct — there must be both integration and differentiation to give rise to diverse states and experiences. A conscious system must be more than a collection of independent parts, and it must form a whole that has a state that cannot be fully explained by looking at each part separately.

A major issue with proving such hypotheses is that researchers have often tested them in ways that lack true neutrality and rigour. A 2022 analysis of hundreds of experiments found that research into consciousness has often been done in ways that pre-emptively bias the results in support of a particular theory3. This has made it a challenge to directly compare studies of consciousness, according to Christof Koch, a consciousness researcher at the Allen Institute for Brain Science in Seattle, Washington, who has studied the topic for decades.

“People become very attached to their theories, and that confirmation bias can sometimes get in the way of an honest, collaborative effort,” he says.

Lucia Melloni, a cognitive neuroscientist at the Ruhr University Bochum in Germany, recently led a first-of-its-kind effort to force a direct comparison of the two schools of thought. She brought together proponents of both theories, as well as neutral participants, and asked them to agree in advance to a set of experiments and predictions. The group probed foundational assumptions of both theories4 using three measurement techniques — EEG; functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which tracks brain activity by detecting tiny changes in blood flow; and magnetoencephalography (MEG), which measures magnetic fields produced by the brain’s electrical currents.

Plants lack brains, but are capable of decision-making and problem-solving.Credit: Jason Milligan/Courtesy of Understory

One of the main differences between the two ideas is which part of the brain is considered most essential to the act of being. The GNWT predicts a sudden ‘ignition’ of widespread brain activity when a stimulus prompts a conscious experience, and so the prefrontal cortex is expected to play an important part because it uses information to form complex behaviours. ITT focuses instead on a ‘hot zone’ located towards the back of the brain that includes parts of the systems responsible for vision, hearing and touch, because it follows that this is where the relevant stimuli converge to generate a full experience.

The team found conscious information represented in both regions. However, the results also challenged important predictions of both theories. The long-lasting activity predicted by the IIT to occur in the back of the cortex was not clearly represented, and the ignition expected by the GNWT was limited. As such, the study did not settle the debate, instead suggesting that both theories might offer parts of an answer.

Melloni doesn’t see this as a failure, and considers such results the most exciting outcome. “I’m happy with what we found because neither theory was left untouched,” she says. “Having your predictions confirmed doesn’t leave you anywhere to grow, whereas having your thinking challenged makes you do better science.”

One way that scientists are attempting to expand their thinking is through interdisciplinary collaborations, drawing evidence from fields as distant as plant and non-human animal biology, robotics and even the search for extraterrestrial life to flesh out the conditions under which consciousness can arise. It’s not certain, for instance, that brains — or even neurons — are required. Astrobiologists have long been searching for sentient life, yet given the expanse of the known Universe, they cannot reasonably assume it will look anything like us.

Manchester United’s search for a possible successor to Michael Carrick appears to be widening, with Stuttgart boss Sebastian Hoeness now emerging as a serious name under consideration.

Carrick eased some pressure with the recent 3-2 Champions League win over Roma, but United’s hierarchy are still assessing alternatives after a poor start to the season.

Eddie Howe has repeatedly been linked with the job, yet fresh reports suggest senior figures at Old Trafford are not fully convinced he is the right long-term choice.

According to The Independent, United are much less sold on Howe than previous reports have suggested and have also discussed Hoeness as a potential option.

The Stuttgart coach is highly regarded for his work in Germany, although there are concerns about whether moving straight into the Man United job would represent too big a step.

Hoeness remains under contract with Stuttgart until 2029 and does not have a release clause, meaning United would likely need to pay significant compensation to appoint him.

Meanwhile, Howe remains firmly in the conversation. CaughtOffside reported that the former Newcastle boss is ready to take the United job immediately if Carrick is dismissed.

From United’s perspective, Hoeness is an interesting alternative because he would represent a more modern, long-term appointment rather than a safer Premier League choice.

Howe offers experience, understands English football and would probably be easier to appoint. He also has admirers inside Old Trafford and has previously indicated that the opportunity would interest him.

Hoeness, however, may have the higher ceiling. His Stuttgart side are known for aggressive pressing, intelligent positional play and strong player development, all qualities United have been trying to build into their football structure.

The risk is obvious. United have already seen how difficult it can be for a highly rated coach to step into the pressure of Old Trafford without Premier League experience.

That makes this a fascinating decision for INEOS. Howe would be the safer option, while Hoeness would feel like the more ambitious one.

For now, Carrick remains in charge, but United’s continued work behind the scenes suggests the club are preparing carefully in case results force them to act.

#1343. Portugal boss Jorge Jesus claims Cristiano Ronaldo did NOT tell him he was retiring from international duty after fallout with superstar: 'I found out the same time as you'

Published: 16:01 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 16:09 EDT, 6 November 2026

Portugal boss Jorge Jesus insists he does not 'feel guilty' about Cristiano Ronaldo's international retirement and had no idea it was coming.

Ronaldo's explosive row with Jesus that escalated after he was left on the bench for a Nations League game and climaxed with the 41-year-old publishing a long statement hammering his manager, left their relationship in tatters.

And on Thursday, weeks after the dispute, Ronaldo announced his retirement from Portugal duty, bringing a sad end to his career on the international stage.

Jesus has now spoken for the first time about it, saying at a press conference: 'I don't feel guilty about anything regarding his departure. I respect his decision and, as such, his history cannot be ignored.

'I will never do that. Because he will always be a symbol, and I have built a strong friendship with him over this year and a half. Sporting-wise, he has now made another decision, and I greatly respect his decision.'

When asked if he thought he was the reason for Ronaldo's retirement, the 72-year-old added: 'No... Maybe I rushed things, but not because of me. It was in his head that, with more or less call-ups, this was going to happen. It was always going to be during my tenure.

Jorge Jesus, pictured at a press conference on Friday, said he did not feel guilty about Cristiano Ronaldo's international retirement

'I didn't speak to Ronaldo because I was thinking about calling him up. From that moment on, I was going to have time to talk to him.'

And Jesus insisted he had no idea why Ronaldo chose now to quit, adding: 'You have to ask him... The absolute certainty I have is that Cris worked with me for a year. We were happy at the club where we were, we were champions. I respect his decision at this moment.

'He would always have been with me throughout all these years that we were going to work together. He was the one who would decide. I don't know why he made that decision. What I do know is that he knew his time was coming, he was the one who would choose. And he chose. Only he can answer that better than I can.'

Ronaldo scored a world record 146 goals in 234 games for Portugal and won the 2016 European Championship as well as two Nations League titles.

But he will not add to those achievements now – instead stepping away after 23 years playing for his country.

In his retirement statement, he admitted that he had at times 'failed' and revealed that his decision was difficult, but felt proud of his work and willing to hand over the number seven jersey.

His final minutes in a Portugal shirt came against Wales in September, when he played 67 minutes in a 1-0 Nations League win over Wales.

After being left on the bench for their subsequent match against Norway, Ronaldo had a row with manager Jesus and flew away from Portugal's camp via his private jet.

Ronaldo never reached a World Cup final and cried after Portugal were knocked out by Spain in the last 16 over the summer

Marking his retirement, he wrote: 'To the people of Portugal, the day has come to return the number 7 jersey of our national team. I never felt it was exclusively mine. But for 23 years, I had the privilege and the responsibility to wear it, to defend it, and to take it with me to stadiums all over the world.

'Today has come the moment to hand it over to the future. It was not an easy decision, because some decisions are not made just with the head, they are also made with the heart.

'I was always demanding of myself. I always wanted more, I always believed we could go further. And I gave everything I had for this jersey. There were perfect afternoons and nights, there were victories I will never forget.

'There were defeats that even today I find hard to remember. I also failed, I also suffered, there were also moments when I was not able to give the Portuguese people what they so desired. But I never gave up. And above all, I never stopped feeling proud to represent Portugal.

'Throughout these years, I learned very simple things. Goals pass, trophies stay in museums, records end up being broken. But there is something that time can never erase: the place we occupy in people's hearts.

'If I ever made you happy, if ever a goal of mine made you hug someone, forget a problem, or simply feel proud of our country, then it was all worth it. Because being Portuguese is also that. We suffer together, we get up together.

'If I got this far, it was because we were always hand in hand. And to the Portuguese, to all Portuguese people scattered around the world, I want to tell you one last thing. There is an image I will always carry with me: the moment the national anthem begins. I look around, I see my teammates, I see the stands, I see children, mothers, fathers, and grandfathers, I see Portuguese people who came from so far just to be there.

'And during those minutes, we stop being different. There are no clubs, there are no colors, there are no classes, there are no professions, there are no opinions. There is only one passion: Portugal.'

There will be questions over the way Ronaldo's international career has ended – to the public, it appears to be on rather bitter terms.

Ronaldo was livid after being left on the bench despite warming-up for Portugal's Nations League win over Norway on September 27 – the first time he has been an unused substitute during his 23-year international career.

The highlight of his Portugal career was lifting the 2016 European Championship, even if he got injured in the final

That led to him skipping three training sessions and abandoning the camp for Portugal's last two matches of the international break, fleeing to Spain via private jet.

He did not even watch their next match against Norway because he was soaring away on his plane with his family.

The former Manchester United star was vexed at how Jesus had handled his press conference after leaving him on the bench.

Ronaldo insisted that Jesus had broken a promise to apologise to the 'Portuguese people' and his team-mates for not bringing him on.

He claimed he had been guaranteed 30 minutes of football against Norway after the Portuguese FA persuaded him not to retire following the World Cup.

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner even offered to retire if that was what the coach and head of Portuguese FA wanted, only for them to reiterate their desire to have him.

But most hurtfully, Ronaldo released a stinging 1,996-word statement accusing Jesus of 'broken promises'. He said the manager had agreed to deliver an eight-point mea culpa taking responsibility for leaving him on the bench after a supposed pact to play him.

Jesus did concede it was a mistake to make him warm up but gave a different narrative of events, saying: 'The match in Norway was not part of the plan I drew up for him. However, I felt that he had managed to recover physically from the first match and I warned him that I might have to use him. Cristiano agreed.'

In the end, Ronaldo was fined £215 by the Portuguese FA and technically banned for a month – though that was backdated, making him free for their upcoming fixtures. But fans – and the man himself – will now have to embrace the next chapter as Portugal aim to move on without the most illustrious player in their history.

#1342. Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”

The veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

Michael Carrick has admitted he has received no guarantees over his Manchester United future beyond Sunday’s Premier League meeting with Aston Villa.

The United head coach remains under significant pressure despite Tuesday’s dramatic 3-2 Champions League comeback victory over Roma.

That result finally ended a lengthy winless run, but it has not completely removed doubts surrounding his position at Old Trafford.

With the November international break beginning immediately after the Villa game, speculation has naturally increased that United’s hierarchy could use the two-week pause to reassess the managerial situation.

Speaking during his pre-match press conference, Carrick was directly asked whether the club had told him he would still be in charge after the international break.

“No, I’ve just carried on as absolute normal,” he replied, according to Man United’s official website.

Carrick also insisted he was not approaching the Villa fixture with uncertainty, saying his focus remained entirely on preparing his players and building momentum from the Roma victory.

The situation is still delicate. United gave Carrick additional time after the damaging 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth, but they have won only once in their last ten matches across all competitions.

Carrick’s calm public stance is understandable, but Sunday feels like another important test.

The win over Roma showed that his players are still capable of responding under pressure. The challenge now is proving it was the start of a recovery rather than another isolated result.

United are also continuing to assess alternatives. CaughtOffside reported that Eddie Howe is ready to take the job immediately if United decide to make a change, while Julian Nagelsmann remains another candidate.

David Ornstein has previously explained that United genuinely wanted Carrick to have more time rather than simply keeping him because alternatives were unavailable.

That support matters, but it clearly is not unconditional.

A convincing victory over Villa could strengthen Carrick’s position significantly heading into the break. Another damaging defeat, however, would inevitably bring the managerial debate straight back to the forefront.

#1340. Serie A | Parma 1-2 Bologna: Ducali’s Derby hope ruined by early red card

Parma were down to 10 men for practically all of this local derby, yet were only beaten 2-1 by Bologna thanks to Arthur Theate and a Riccardo Orsolini penalty, a fourth straight victory.

This was an intriguing Emilia-Romagna Derby between two sides who already changed coach early in the campaign. Alberto Gilardino was celebrating his first victory on the Parma bench with a 3-0 away to Atalanta on Monday, but missed Adrian Bernabé and Dominik Drobnic.

Bologna were on a roll under Raffaele Palladino of three straight wins, even with Jay Enem, Emil Holm and Lorenzo De Silvestri sidelined, but were boosted by the return of Roberto Piccoli to the bench.

In the opening minute, Giovanni Daffara had to scramble the ball round the near post when Federico Bernardeschi’s snapshot took a double deflection.

The game changed after eight minutes when Abdoulaye Ndiaye and Jens Odgaard went down in a tangle just outside the penalty area, the referee originally waving play on to suggest they were fouling each other. However, he changed his mind following a VAR review, as Odgaard having a handful of shorts was considered insufficient to rescue Ndiaye from a red card for DOGSO (Denial of a Goal Scoring Opportunity).

Bologna started to pour forward against 10-man Parma, with a Juan Miranda volley charged down by Benja Cremaschi, and a couple of headers from Odgaard and Nicolò Casale just off target.

David Romero fell very awkwardly after a Casale sliding tackle and seemed to dislocate his shoulder, so had to be substituted.

Enrico Delprato’s header flashed wide of the far post on a free kick, but Bologna were also forced into a change for Miranda’s muscular injury.

Substitute Samuel Mbangula’s curler was palmed out from under the bar, then Daffara was tested by Odgaard at the near post, also parrying a Tommaso Pobega strike.

Federico Bernardeschi’s acrobatic volley on a Nicolò Cambiaghi cross forced another strong Daffara save at the dawn of the second half, while Cambiaghi’s free header was straight at the Parma goalkeeper.

The siege finally paid off when Cambiaghi stood up a cross from the right for the Theate diving header from six yards to break the deadlock.

Moments later, the referee pointed to the spot for a Mandela Keita foul on Bernardeschi, but VAR clarified the contact was just outside the penalty area.

Daffara needed quick reactions after a mad scramble in the six-yard box on a corner, yet Parma nearly equalised on the hour mark when El Bilal Touré started the run from midfield against the entire Bologna defence and was only denied by Lukasz Skorupski’s trailing leg.

Penalty appeals were initially rejected for an incredibly risky Touré tackle from behind on Cambiaghi, a decision that was changed following the VAR review which showed he made no contact with the ball. Riccardo Orsolini converted with power despite Daffara guessing the right way.

VAR got involved again at the other end when Giovanni Fabbian tried an audacious backwards flick from six yards on a set play and was caught by Martin Vitik in the process. A penalty was awarded following a review, and Vincent Sierro converted to keep 10-man Parma in the game.

So did Daffara, getting down to push a Bernardeschi free kick round the far post, so in added time Christian Ordonez saw his screamer fly just over the bar.

It was 10-man Parma who pushed to the bitter end, but were unable to turn the situation around.

Theate 53 (B), Orsolini pen 72 (B), Sierro pen 81 (P)

#1339. Rangers hitman Ryan Naderi is finding his groove at the ideal time... and he could hold the key in Ibrox trophy hunt

Published: 15:06 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 16:27 EDT, 6 November 2026

Back in February, Danny Rohl’s decision to tell the Rangers supporters that his latest signing Ryan Naderi reminded him of a certain Thomas Muller was met with widespread derision.

Quite right too. In truth, those comments still sound every bit as silly as they did nine months ago.

However, while that will surely be the first and last time Naderi is likened to the German World Cup winner, Rohl at least appears to have been proven right in his assertion that the frontman had the tools to ultimately be a success at Ibrox.

Clearly, he saw something the rest of us couldn’t.

You would have got long odds on the newly-capped Czech international still being at the club by the time the summer transfer window shut in early September, such was the general feeling towards the big man after a thoroughly underwhelming start to life in Glasgow.

That Rangers were so keen to pay Hansa Rostock the best part of £5million to bring him over from the German third tier appeared somewhat foolish given that Naderi would go on to find the net just three times across all competitions, with two of those coming in an 8-0 rout of Queen’s Park in the Scottish Cup.

Naderi's winning goal against Aberdeen last weekend took his tally for the season to eight

Simply put, he played more like a headless chicken than a reliable Rangers striker.

The summer departure of the man who convinced the club to push the boat out to get him, followed by the arrival of Derek McInnes — not to mention new club skipper Lawrence Shankland — suggested his days may have already been numbered.

You’d have done well to find any Rangers fan who would have objected either.

But, in a very short time, Naderi has put the hard yards in to establish himself as an integral part of this Rangers team. In fact, he’s almost undroppable these days.

His late goal against Aberdeen last weekend to book Rangers’ place in the Premier Sports Cup final against Hibs next month was his eighth in 16 appearances this season.

Let’s not pretend that those numbers would be quite as impressive had the likes of Shankland and Youssef Chermiti been on the pitch rather than on the treatment table. Naderi probably knows that himself.

But all he can do in their absence is take advantage of the opportunity offered to him, and it’s so far so good in that sense.

It’s evident that he is a man playing with confidence, and his displays are night-and-day from what we saw last season.

McInnes has to take a fair share of the credit for the role he has played in Naderi turning his Ibrox career around. The manager’s style suits him to a tee.

Of course, there are all sorts of nuances and intricate details that go into his tactical ideology, but the general idea is pretty simple: Get the ball forward as quickly as possible.

Manager Derek McInnes has managed to get the best out of his Czech striker in recent months

There is very little faffing around in midfield under McInnes’ Rangers. None of this tippy-tappy nonsense. It was the same when he was in charge at Kilmarnock, and certainly a huge reason behind Hearts’ success last season too.

And Naderi — alongside Kevin Kelsy — is benefiting from a more direct approach which aims to turn the opposition around at every opportunity. It’s proven fairly effective until this point.

You would suspect the chances will keep coming with players such as Kim Min-su and Badredine Bouanani providing the ammunition, with the latter in particular really coming on to a game in recent weeks after taking some time to find his feet since making the loan switch from VfB Stuttgart.

Part of Naderi’s problem last season was that he was spending too much time outside the box in an effort to get involved in the build-up. Too eager to impress, perhaps.

In this team, he doesn’t need to do that anywhere near as often.

There’s no reason why he can’t hit double figures this year. In fact, it would now be considered a major disappointment if he failed to do so.

He’ll have a chance to boost his numbers on Saturday evening when he lines up against St Mirren. And he will no doubt fancy doing exactly that, having registered a goal and two assists against Craig McLeish’s men earlier this season.

With Celtic failing to extend their lead at the top of the table last weekend after falling to defeat in Falkirk, Rangers can move to within a point ahead of the defending champions’ meeting with Kilmarnock on Sunday.

They will need to be a damn sight better than they have been on their travels of late to do so, however. Back-to-back 2-2 draws on the road at Dundee and Hearts could prove costly further down the line in what’s shaping up to be a tight title race. They could have easily lost both.

They simply can’t afford to drop any more points, especially with Celtic continuing to look so vulnerable.

Rangers can't afford to drop more points after back-to-back away draws at Dundee and Hearts

You would assume Martin O’Neill’s men will find their groove eventually, so it is imperative that Rangers stay within striking distance until they face off again in the new year.

It should be an intriguing tussle in Paisley. The Buddies have earned plaudits for the way in which they have attempted to move away from the style employed under former boss Stephen Robinson.

And they have demonstrated on multiple occasions this season that they can be hard to stop when in full flow. They certainly gave Celtic a scare back in September before succumbing to a narrow 2-1 loss.

But they have undoubtedly taken a step back of late, winning just once in their last eight league fixtures.

Keeping Naderi quiet will be key to stopping the rot. There’s a statement you couldn’t possibly have envisaged reading not too long ago.

Jamie Redknapp believes Arsenal could be heading towards another Premier League title after Mikel Arteta’s side opened up a six-point advantage over Manchester City.

The defending champions have won nine of their opening 10 league matches, while City’s challenge has suddenly faltered following three consecutive defeats.

Arsenal’s latest 1-0 victory over Hull City moved them onto 27 points, with Martin Odegaard scoring the decisive goal, while City were beaten 3-1 by Nottingham Forest.

Speaking on Sky Sports following City’s defeat, Redknapp admitted he currently struggles to see anybody stopping Arsenal.

“I don’t really see anything else other than Arsenal running away with this title at the moment,” he said. “I know it’s really early but I just think they’re so much better than everyone else in every single area.”

Redknapp surprisingly identified Brighton rather than City, Liverpool or Chelsea as Arsenal’s most credible challengers.

“If you look at the league table, I think right now, probably the one you’d point to, and I never thought I’d say this at the start of the year, but it’s Brighton,” he added.

Brighton currently sit third with 19 points from nine matches and would move above City by beating Brentford on Sunday.

Redknapp’s confidence is understandable. Arsenal have won five successive league matches and conceded just five goals in 10 games, while City’s three consecutive losses have produced a remarkable nine-point swing in Arsenal’s favour.

City have recovered from difficult periods before, while Brighton’s excellent start will face a much greater test as the season progresses. Arsenal themselves know from previous title challenges how quickly momentum can change.

The difference this time is that Arteta’s side look increasingly comfortable winning without playing their best football. If that resilience continues, Redknapp’s prediction may not seem quite so bold by the spring.

#1337. Replacing the neurons that Parkinson’s destroys

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Laura Dattaro is a science journalist in Maplewood, New Jersey.

In people with Parkinson’s disease, neurons in the brain that produce dopamine are continuously lost. Without the neurotransmitter, which is crucial for movement, control of motor function begins to break down, resulting in symptoms such as tremors — one of the hallmarks of Parkinson’s.

Replacing dopamine is the goal of many treatments. Since the 1960s, that’s been done with a drug called levodopa, an amino acid that the brain converts to dopamine. But that conversion is carried out by the dopamine neurons that Parkinson’s eats away at. Lose too many, and the medication can no longer reliably control symptoms.

Some researchers have therefore long been eyeing the possibility of restoring those neurons. That entails growing them outside the brain and then injecting them through holes drilled into each side of the skull. The hope is that the cells will take root and begin to replenish the dwindling supply of dopamine.

Nearly four decades after such a transplant was first attempted, the work is beginning to pay off. Since early 2025, four phase I and II clinical trials have reported early results showing that the treatment is largely safe, with some people reporting improved motor skills and less ‘off’ time, during which their medication is ineffective. Off time can result from small daily changes, such as to diet, as well as the loss of dopamine neurons over time. Some of those treatments are moving into phase III trials for efficacy. More trials are in the works, raising cautious hopes that a new treatment for the disease is on the horizon. One of the first trials to test the cells in people with Parkinson’s was successful enough that the treatment is already available in Japan, albeit under strict regulatory oversight.

“This is such an exciting place to be,” says Claire Henchcliffe, a neurologist at the University of California, Irvine. “These are first-in-human trials. We’ve never had any products like these before.”

Despite the momentum, no one thinks that the treatment is ready for large-scale use. The trials so far have been small, with no control groups, and were designed to measure safety, not effectiveness. They’ve opened up a host of questions for researchers to investigate, including which type of cell to transplant, how many to deliver and where to inject them. There’s also work to be done to understand how the brain responds to its new members.

Transplanting foreign cells requires around one year of immunosuppression, and the brain surgery itself carries risks, including haemorrhage and infection. But the trials move cell transplants from a theory requiring proof to an early-stage treatment needing development, says molecular neurobiologist Kwang-Soo Kim at McLean Hospital in Belmont, Massachusetts, who completed the first transplant of neurons derived from the cells of a person with Parkinson’s in 20171. The question now, Kim says, is, “How can we optimize them?”

To begin down the road to approval, researchers led by Jun Takahashi at Kyoto University, Japan, injected cells grown from donor tissue — known as allogenic cells — into the brains of seven people with Parkinson’s. The procedure seemed to be safe: none developed tumours, a concern of transferring immature cells into the body2.

Positron emission tomography (PET) scans showed that, two years after surgery and around 9 months after immunosuppression was stopped, on average, participants had more dopamine in the putamen — the part of the brain into which the neurons are injected — than they did before the procedure. This showed that the transplanted cells remained biologically active, even after immunosuppression was stopped. The movement symptoms of some of the participants also showed signs of improvement.

On the basis of the results, the Japanese government gave the team conditional approval for the cell transplantations. This regulatory stage gives people access to the therapy, and the costs are covered by the national health insurance system, while researchers closely observe and document their progress — similar to being in a phase III clinical trial in the United States. Full approval will take seven years, Takahashi says, during which his team will monitor safety and efficacy.

The concept behind stem-cell therapy for Parkinson’s was first tested in people in the 1980s, when researchers transplanted dopaminergic neurons taken from 8–10-week-old aborted fetuses into the brains of people with Parkinson’s. The participants showed improvements in their motor symptoms. After three years, one participant had improved enough to stop taking levodopa. Nearly two decades after treatment, two individuals still had the motor improvements seen in the years immediately after surgery and had stopped taking medication more than a decade earlier.

Dopamine neurons are lost in Parkinson’s.Credit: Janko Kajtez/Parmar lab

But this approach has a major flaw: fetal tissue is rare and difficult to obtain, and using cells derived from it in research is legally and ethically complex, says Malin Parmar, a neurobiologist at Lund University in Sweden. Parmar has worked on the TransEuro study, which used fetal tissue for the treatment of Parkinson’s3. “You can never upscale them into reliable therapies,” Parmar says.

But a 2006 discovery4 of how to revert any mature tissue into stem cells — dubbed induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) — and then coax them into becoming any other cell was a game-changer. Suddenly it was possible to imagine creating vast amounts of cells for research and medicine, and it didn’t take long for researchers to start probing the best ways to turn iPSCs into dopaminergic neurons — work that is now making its way to people. “It has turned from, ‘This has been done before, it won’t work,” to suddenly, ‘Oh boy, I can’t keep up with all the clinical trials,” Henchcliffe says.

In 2023, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared the way for Sumitomo Pharma in Osaka, Japan, which makes the cell product used by Takahashi, to conduct trials in the United States. Three people have already received transplants, says Joseph Ciacci, a neurosurgeon at the University of California, San Diego, who is leading the trial. His team aims to treat eight people.

Ciacci is hopeful that the brains of people he has treated can recover lost function after the transplants. The new neurons could be a buffer against treatments such as levodopa becoming less effective over time. “I feel very excited about it,” he says.

Sumitomo says it has also begun a larger trial that will enrol dozens of people, including a control group that will receive sham surgery. The company aims to compare the cells used in both trials and launch its therapy in the United States by 2032.

Three other trials have reported results so far, using a mix of cell types. All have a small sample size — fewer than 15 people — and none of them has a control group. The results should therefore be interpreted cautiously, researchers say. Still, all of the studies that have reported data met their safety endpoints and showed early signs of clinical benefit.

A trial involving 12 people, co-led by Henchcliffe, reported similar results to those of Takahashi’s team, including increased dopamine uptake at 18 months measured using PET and improvements in motor scores5. The trial was sponsored by stem-cell specialist BlueRock Therapeutics in Cambridge, Massachusetts, which is a subsidiary of multinational pharmaceutical company Bayer.

Blue Rock’s cell product, called bemdaneprocel, received the FDA’s Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy (RMAT) designation in 2024 and the Japanese health ministry’s Pioneering Regenerative Medical Product designation in December 2025. The team is currently enrolling participants in a phase III trial that will include a sham-surgery control group; it aims to transplant cells into 102 people in the United States, Canada and Australia and monitor their motor function for 18 months.

A third trial in eight individuals, run by the biotech company Aspen Neuroscience in San Diego, California, used dopaminergic neurons generated from the participants’ own cells, known as autologous cells. The cell recipients showed motor improvements, and several were able to reduce their dose of levodopa, according to results presented at the International Conference on Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s Diseases in March.

Dopaminergic progenitor cells are injected into the brain of a person with Parkinson’s.Credit: Kyoto University Hospital

The company has now completed transplants in another seven people with its cell product, called sasineprocel, and received RMAT designation in July. It plans to begin a phase III trial of the treatment this year.

In the same month, Parmar and her colleagues reported the first results of a trial, called STEM-PD, in which they transplanted neurons derived from embryonic stem cells into eight patients. The participants showed “good early signs” of symptom improvement, Parmar says. Six of the seven people who completed the follow-up period opted to reduce their dose of levodopa as a result. Similar to the other trials, none grew tumours or had other serious reactions to the cells, but one participant died ten weeks after the transplant owing to an infection they developed while taking immunosuppressive drugs6.

Taken together, Parmar says, the trial results show that the transplanted cells survive and don’t generate tumours. But more people need to be followed up for longer periods before the treatment can truly be called effective, especially given that treatments such as levodopa already exist, she says. She recommends that researchers adopt an approach of skynda långsamt, a Swedish phrase meaning to rush slowly. “What we have is really hopeful and very promising,” Parmar says. “But the expectations are super high.”

While trials seek evidence that the approach works, researchers are also trying to get a better understanding of how the brain responds to allogeneic and autologous transplants, with an eye to further boosting safety and efficacy.

Allogenic transplants require that people undergo immunosuppression, generally for one year, to prevent the brain from attacking or rejecting the cells. But some researchers are working on a way to do away with that need by genetically ‘cloaking’ allogenic cells — editing certain genes to hide the cells from the immune system7.

Last year, a team led by researchers at the Florey Institute in Melbourne, Australia, coaxed human stem cells into overexpressing genes that modulate the immune system. They then grew the cells into neurons and implanted them into a rat model of Parkinson’s. The rats that received the edited cells mounted less of an immune response than did those that received unedited neurons, and showed greater improvement in motor symptoms8.

Autologous cells don’t require such immunosuppression. But they do have their own drawbacks. Because they need to be generated for each person, individuals need to wait months before the cells can be implanted — a particular problem for people with Parkinson’s, whose neurons are continuously being destroyed. Using individualized cells for each transplant also introduces variation that makes measuring outcomes in clinical trials difficult, Parmar says. It’s more expensive than a treatment using allogenic cells, too, which researchers hope will eventually be available in large, off-the-shelf batches.

It’s even possible, says Parmar, that autologous cells from a person with Parkinson’s might be innately susceptible to developing the disease after transplantation, meaning that the treatment’s success could be shorter-lived. In 2020, Parmar and her team transplanted neurons derived from either an embryonic stem-cell line or a person with a gene mutation linked to Parkinson’s into a rat model of the disease. Both types of cell survived and rats receiving either type had improved symptoms. But in the rats that received the cells with the Parkinson’s gene, the transplanted grafts showed early signs of disease development9. Regardless of the source, turning immature brain cells into a viable, accessible treatment will require improvements to the processes for generating them en masse. Researchers are hoping that automation and standardization will bring down both the cost and the time needed to produce them. Some draw comparisons to full-genome sequencing: the first full human genome cost hundreds of millions of dollars to sequence, but today it can be done for about US$1,000.

Work is also needed to improve the survival of implanted cells. Although the trials — which are testing both high and low cell doses — show that some cells do take root in the brain and become productive dopamine-producing neurons, many more do not. In the BlueRock trial, for example, researchers delivered 900,000 cells to each side of the brain of people in the low-dose group, but they expected that only 150,000 cells per side would survive. In the high-dose group, participants received 2.7 million cells on each side of the brain in an attempt to have 300,000 survive5.

“After the cells are put into brain, you have no more control,” says Su-Chun Zhang, director of the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys, a non-profit research institute in La Jolla, California. “They are on their own.”

Some researchers who are trying to improve cell survival think that the environment into which cells are transplanted might matter — just as the quality of a plot of land can affect a gardener’s outcomes. “We have spent many, many years to improve the seed,” Kim says. “But we didn’t pay attention to the soil.”

Like fertilizing soil, preparing the brain before the transplant could help. Some groups, for example, are exploring whether injecting specific growth factors along with the cells might coax them into becoming mature dopamine neurons. And in 2023, Kim and his team discovered a phenomenon they called ‘needle trauma’ in mice, in which the brain responds to placebo injections with an immune response that causes inflammation and kills brain cells. Transplanting immune cells called T cells along with the placebo injection suppressed the response10.

Kim is also concerned about the potential for cells to acquire mutations during the reprogramming and manufacturing process — and the potential long-term effects of such genetic changes, given that the cells might remain in a person’s brain for decades. “Stem-cell therapies are living products,” Kim says. Questions about such genomic integrity highlight the careful balance researchers must strike when pursuing a desperately sought after and potentially life-changing treatment but one that researchers still know so little about. That was obvious to Kim in 2020, when he was inundated with calls, e-mails and letters from people with Parkinson’s and their families after the publication of preliminary results for the first person to receive his transplant.

“We have to keep optimistic, and we have to give them hope,” Kim says. “But very informed hope.”

#1336. Napoli chief De Laurentiis: ‘Here is why I cancelled Allegri press conference’

Napoli President Aurelio De Laurentiis confirms the report he cancelled Max Allegri’s press conference 10 minutes before it was due to begin, but insists ‘there’s no controversy.’

The squad was put into a training retreat from Friday to prepare for Sunday’s Serie A showdown with current leaders Lazio.

This was a response to the recent defeats to Juventus and FC Porto, capitulating 4-1 in the Champions League on Wednesday evening.

Allegri was all ready to speak in the press room this afternoon, with the journalists assembled and equipment set up when it was suddenly announced the whole event was cancelled.

“There is no controversy at Napoli,” wrote President De Laurentiis on his social media channels after reports he was the one who made the call to cancel.

“When I realised that we were about to hold yet another press conference, I preferred to block it. Why? Because I don’t think press conferences are necessary before every game, considering we play every three days.

“We are in a training retreat, and we must avoid any kind of distraction to take away the players’ concentration on the match. When we go into a retreat, there must be total protection.”

Inevitably, this will further fuel reports that De Laurentiis is losing confidence in Allegri, the coach he chose to replace Antonio Conte over the summer even after the tactician was sacked by Milan for missing out on the top four.

Napoli have struggled badly this season, emerging with five wins, two draws and seven defeats, scoring 23 goals and conceding 24.

#1335. Is Jobe Bellingham England's next big thing who shares his older brother's 'X-Factor' - or a 'problem child' whose dad blows up at his bosses? Inside the rise of the 21-year-old after first call-up

Published: 09:16 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 16:31 EDT, 6 November 2026

For years, Jobe Bellingham has been in the shadows of his older brother Jude.

Now, for the first time since they were children, the duo are poised to perform on the same stage. Only this time it won't be under the lampposts of Stourbridge, but the floodlights at Wembley.

Jobe, 21, has been called up to England's senior squad for the first time and is often described in similar terms to his elder sibling: relentlessly ambitious, focused, and a quick learner who is wise beyond his years.

'You have to have an X-Factor and Jobe does,' said Regis Le Bris, his old manager at Sunderland.

That X-Factor appears to run in the Bellingham blood. Earlier this week Jude was unveiled as the new underwear heart-throb for Calvin Klein, channelling his inner David Beckham in a smouldering photoshoot. No pressure, Jobe.

Their main difference on the pitch is that Jobe, while versatile, tends to occupy a deeper-lying role in midfield – and that actually increases the chances of Thomas Tuchel fielding them together. There is every chance that, against Croatia or Spain next week, we will see just the fourth pair of brothers to feature for England since the Second World War.

Jude and Jobe Bellingham's dream of playing for England together may finally come true

The duo grew up playing together and both joined the Birmingham City academy (Instagram: judebellingham)

The duo visited the Spanish Grand Prix in September with matching shirts and haircuts

They share a close relationship and in September were VIP guests of McLaren for the Spanish Grand Prix, posing for photographs in matching blue shirts and identical haircuts, a mischievous double act.

If you were a few pints deep in the Formula One hospitality area, you'd be forgiven for thinking they were the same bloke – especially when their footballing trajectories are so similar.

Jobe began his career at Birmingham City, like Jude, before moving to Sunderland and now Borussia Dortmund, where his brother also played. Jobe, who is two years younger than his superstar brother, is now in his second full season with the Westphalia giants.

He has previously admitted his trepidation at following in Jude's footsteps, once telling the German club's in-house media channel: 'I was biased against joining Borussia Dortmund for a very long time.

'I had anxieties, fears, and you want to be your own man. But I don't think I should let those stop me from making the right decision.'

The comparisons are inevitable, though, when you share the same name and your potential also happens to be through the ceiling. It is a theme Jobe will simply have to contend with wherever he roams.

In Dortmund's 2-2 draw with Bayern Munich on Saturday, the resemblance was striking as he delivered a standout performance – even having the ball in the back of the net, though his goal was ruled out for a Carney Chukwuemeka foul.

At one stage, Bellingham backheeled the ball over Aleksandar Pavlovic, won the ball back off Dayot Upamecano, drifted past Pavlovic with a skill that left him on one knee, and drove about 30 yards towards goal before firing a shot just over the bar.

They would be just the fourth pair of brother to play for England since the Second World War

Jude and Jobe are pictured together at a Louis Vuitton Paris Fashion Week show in 2023

In that ten-second flash, he displayed the sort of tenacity, ingenuity, and swagger which we have come to associate with Jude.

While not as brazen on the surface as Jude, Jobe perhaps gets some of his confidence from their father Mark.

The brothers were introduced to football by their dad, a retired police sergeant who also scored 700 goals in non-league.

Raising his sons in the West Midlands alongside their mother Denise, Mark gave them tips on how to improve and how to deal with the pressures of football. Jude even describes his father as his first footballing hero.

The crackerjack duo have always competed to see who can be the most precocious. Jude became Birmingham City's youngest-ever player when he debuted for them in 2019. When Jobe made his bow for them in 2022, he did so just 69 days older.

He earned his move to Sunderland after just 26 games and was a hit on Wearside. In his second campaign, he won the Championship Young Player of the Season award and helped them to promotion via the play-offs.

Manager Le Bris was breathless in his praise. 'There are many [qualities], there is a long list,' he said. 'Probably his ambition is one of the first ideas I have when I think about Jobe.

'He is very ambitious but this ambition is not naive. It is connected with what he is doing every day in training and every game on the pitch.

Jude pictured with his brother Jobe, father Mark, and mother Denise upon signing for Borussia Dortmund in 2020

'He has many good qualities as a footballer. He is very powerful and he understands the game very well. He is really interested in the game and, because of that, he is able to improve with experiences. He can learn very quickly.

'He is older than his age. He has more maturity. He is like an exception in the sport. It is not easy to play at the level he is doing so at his age, but he is doing so well.'

In the summer of 2025, Dortmund got on the blower. They were willing to pay £31million – more than they had for Jude – and put him straight in the squad for the Club World Cup. Dortmund's UK scout is Daniel Dodds, the brother of Mike, who had worked with Jobe in Birmingham's academy and at Sunderland.

'I think he can go to the very top,' Mike told the Northern Echo in 2023. 'Both brothers have a very similar mindset in terms of their relentlessness in their pursuit of where they want to get to.'

Despite the extravagant projections, Jobe's time in Germany's industrial belt has not been entirely smooth. Often he has been left to simmer on the bench, unable to nail down a regular starting spot.

In his first Klassiker experience, he came on only to lose the ball and have Michael Olise's shot deflect in off him. One report described him as a man who looked 'completely stripped of confidence'.

On the opening day of last season against St Pauli, he was hauled off at the break, leading to his father going ballistic and allegedly confronting sporting director Sebastian Kehl. That put Jobe in an awkward spot. He was also sent off for a professional foul against Freiburg.

Amid his struggles to adapt to the Bundesliga, he has copped criticism off the ferocious pundit Dietmar Hamann, who blasted him as a 'problem child' in a column for Sky Sport. 'Young, expensive and, so far, not even half as good as Jude Bellingham,' seethed the former Liverpool midfielder.

Jobe has become a more regular starter since the turn of the year and, in any case, has always been highly thought of in English football circles.

Jobe helped Sunderland to promotion from the Championship - manager Regis Le Bris said he had the 'X-factor'

Lee Carsley made Jobe his captain for the Under-21s and waxed lyrical about him: 'I think he will be an all-round box-to-box player. He can be creative, score goals. I still feel he can score more goals.

'His shooting is excellent, especially in training. He can link and receive in tight areas.'

Carsley added: 'He’s a good example to the rest of the group, the way he conducts himself on and off the pitch, the way he prepares, the influence he has on the rest of the team.

'He’s a player who can grow into that role. We just assume that players understand leadership and how that works. It will be good to add another string to his bow and keep improving his game.'

After his U21s debut against Spain in Cadiz, he was ambushed by people who wanted signatures... on their Real Madrid shirts. It was opportune and distasteful, but reflected the bigger picture: the name Bellingham is associated with Jude.

Now Jobe's moment has come. Tuchel picked him partly because of Carsley jabbering on with praise in his ear over recent months. The noise around him has become unavoidable and, with Alex Scott injured and Myles Lewis-Skelly suspended for the first game, the Three Lions are light in midfield.

'To play with my brother for England that would be the biggest dream of my life. Nothing would even get close to that,' Jude said in 2024. That may soon be a reality.

Liverpool are reportedly preparing for the possibility of life after Alisson Becker, with Porto goalkeeper Diogo Costa emerging as a serious target for 2027.

Alisson’s contract expires next summer, and uncertainty over a renewal has forced Liverpool to think carefully about the next phase of their goalkeeping plans.

Giorgi Mamardashvili is already at the club, while Lucca Brughmans and Armin Pecsi are highly rated internally, but there are doubts over whether any of them are ready to immediately replace one of the best goalkeepers of Liverpool’s modern era.

According to Anfield Watch, Liverpool have identified Diogo Costa as a leading option if Alisson leaves when his deal expires.

The report claims Liverpool admire Costa’s experience, shot-stopping and ability with the ball at his feet, qualities that would fit naturally into Andoni Iraola’s system.

Liverpool are not completely convinced that Mamardashvili is ready to become the undisputed No.1, while Brughmans is still considered one for the future. Pecsi is also viewed as part of a longer-term plan and could be sent out on loan again next season.

Liverpool’s interest in Costa is not entirely new either. CaughtOffside reported earlier this year that the Reds had already been tracking the Portugal international as a potential Alisson successor.

From Liverpool’s perspective, Costa would be a logical replacement.

He is already experienced at Champions League and international level, is comfortable playing out from the back and would arrive ready to compete immediately rather than needing a long adaptation period.

The uncertainty around Alisson has also increased. Iraola admitted this week that he does not know whether the Brazilian will stay, although he made clear that he would like him to continue at Anfield.

That makes succession planning essential rather than premature.

Liverpool could simply promote Mamardashvili, but replacing Alisson with an established goalkeeper such as Costa would reduce the risk of a major drop-off in such a crucial position.

The challenge will be price. Porto have never been an easy club to negotiate with, and Costa remains one of their most valuable players.

Still, if Alisson does leave in 2027, Liverpool will need quality rather than compromise. Costa looks like one of the strongest options available.
