#1333. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is important and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

#1332. D’Amico: ‘Roma learning experience at Manchester United, need new resources’

Roma director Tony D’Amico admits the defeat to Manchester United was ‘a learning experience’ for them, confirming the need to sign ‘a forward who can do damage on the counter-attack’ when leading.

The match with Sassuolo kicks off at the Stadio Olimpico in Rome at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from today’s four Serie A games on the Liveblog.

The Giallorossi are still unbeaten this season in Serie A, but have twice thrown away massive leads in the Champions League for defeats to Real Madrid and now Manchester United.

That Old Trafford collapse from 2-0 up to lose 3-2 confirmed this is a recurring problem, so this evening the pressure is on to get a result against struggling Sassuolo.

“It is a problem we realised towards the end of the transfer session, that we lack a wide forward who has pace and can do damage in those situations on the counter-attack,” D’Amico told Sky Sport Italia.

“We will try to correct that when the January window comes around, so will try to give the coach this extra characteristic that we don’t currently have.”

It has been said that Roma lack experience in the Champions League and that cost them when their heads dropped in those situations.

“In an atmosphere like Old Trafford, the fans make a big difference and they helped turn the tide of that game,” insisted D’Amico.

“What I saw in both the games against Manchester United and Real Madrid was a great Roma side that imposes its style of play on the strongest opponents. There are going to be moments of difficulty in fixtures like this.

“I don’t think enough has been said, partly because we don’t like to court controversy, but the penalty for Manchester United was more than generous. So we did have a moment of difficulty, but that penalty sparked the comeback.

“As I said after the Real Madrid defeat, these are learning experiences for a club that has not been in the Champions League for seven years, it also teaches us what resources we still need to give to the coach in order to continue this progress.”

“We speak with all the international coaches, Koné returned to training this week, we are pleased he is back and it gives us the chance to rest someone who played nine games in 28 days.”

#1331. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

9 - Florian Wirtz's nine chances created from open play against Brentford is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané v Burnley in January 2021 (9) and the most by a player in an away game since Samir Nasri v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Progress. https://t.co/xyMIQP9y5p

One of the advantages of Iraola’s Anfield appointment was his Premier League experience with Bournemouth. The Basque well knows the division and has plenty of positive memories from which to borrow.

However, there will also be some scar tissue, and that certainly is the case with Brentford. Iraola never beat the Bees in seven attempts (five draws, two defeats), a run which included a 4-1 thrashing at the Gtech Community Stadium in his final season at Bournemouth.

It’s back-to-back wins for Chelsea and a rare clean sheet, their first since January. But all thoughts will be with Emi Martinez after his clash of heads with Branthwaite. Hopefully we get some good news on that front soon. Follow the latest updates here.

Enzo Maresca has been looking for opportunities for rest his key players - but Erling Haaland is a player that is impossible to rest. He has scored in his last seven matches and leads Manchester City’s attack again.

But Maresca has changed half of his team from the line-up defeated by Paris St-Germain in the week. Jeremy Doku and City’s first-choice centre-backs are the others to keep their place. The rest are drafted in to face Ipswich, with Matheus Nunes, Nico O’Reilly, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Iliman Ndiaye and Mateo Kovačić are drafted in.

There is also a place for Phil Foden after serving his three-match ban for getting dismissed in the Manchester derby.

Keith Andrews has established a clearly defined, direct style of play which speaks to Brentford’s strengths. His side are third in the Premier League for percentage of passes forward (39.2 per cent) and, coupled with the second-most high turnovers which end in a goal, Brentford have thrived off passages of organised chaos.

To play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

Manchester City’s claim to have “irrefutable evidence” that will overturn their guilty verdict on appeal is based on a trove of emails, letters and bank statements.

A re-examination of Abu Dhabi government documents, receipts and testimony from 24 witnesses – all of which the club believe were wrongly dismissed at the original hearing – will be central in attempts to force a full or partial acquittal or retrial, according to people familiar with the case.

City’s legal team will attempt to demonstrate “fundamental errors” in tests applied by an independent commission to the Premier League’s case that commercial revenue was artificially inflated by £920m. Sources with understanding of City’s case have told Telegraph Sport the club are bullish about their appeal, based on:

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. The result was devastating for all of us, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

“And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

This feels like an extremely treacherous trip for Liverpool and for Andoni Iraola, who has a poor record against Brentford. With Bournemouth, he did not win any of his six matches against today’s opponents.

The good news for Liverpool is that Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai are fit enough to start the game, and that Brentford top scorer Kevin Schade is not. Schade is on the bench after picking up a shoulder injury against Aston Villa last weekend.

Barcola opened his Liverpool account on Wednesday and he will look to continue his goal-scoring form at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Speaking of the France winger, head coach Andoni Iraola said: “I think it’s still very early, especially for him who hasn’t played any minutes in pre-season, he’s kind of been doing pre-season in the first games with us almost [in] official games.

“It’s remarkable because to score three goals in a Champions League game is … not a lot of players can say they have done it.

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. Alisson Becker could be heading towards the end of his Liverpool career, with Fabrizio Romano revealing there is now a serious possibility the Brazilian leaves Anfield when his contract expires next summer.

The 34-year-old has been one of Liverpool’s most important players since arriving from Roma in 2018, but his current deal only runs until June 2027.

With no active renewal talks taking place, the Reds may soon face one of their biggest succession decisions in years.

Speaking on his YouTube channel, Romano explained that Liverpool were aware Alisson considered a move to Juventus earlier in 2026 before deciding to stay for another season.

Romano said Liverpool activated a one-year extension because the club were already going through major changes, with Mohamed Salah, Andy Robertson and other senior figures departing.

Alisson ultimately chose to remain and help during the transition from Arne Slot to Andoni Iraola, but Romano now believes a summer exit is realistic.

“I think it’s a serious possibility,” Romano said when discussing whether this could be Alisson’s final Liverpool season.

Iraola himself has admitted he does not know whether Alisson will stay, although he made clear that he hopes the goalkeeper signs a new deal.

Losing Alisson for nothing would be a huge moment for Liverpool.

Even at 34, he remains one of the defining goalkeepers of his generation and replacing his shot-stopping, distribution and leadership would not be straightforward.

Liverpool are already preparing for that possibility. Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki is being monitored as a potential long-term successor.

Giorgi Mamardashvili is another option already at Anfield, while Liverpool have also been linked with Porto goalkeeper Diogo Costa.

The interesting part is that an Alisson exit is not yet inevitable. Romano stressed that Liverpool could still offer him a new contract if their stance changes.

That decision should not be delayed too long. Allowing one of Liverpool’s greatest modern players to leave without having a clear replacement ready would be a major gamble.

For now, Alisson’s future remains unresolved, but the possibility of a summer farewell feels more realistic than ever.

#1329. He had the world at his feet when he signed for Real Madrid at 13, mixing with Zidane and Ronaldo. Now Jack Harper plays in Italy's Serie D... but he's not giving up on his Scotland dream

Published: 13:06 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 17:10 EDT, 6 November 2026

Whatever the Italian word is for ‘steamie’, the steady migration of Scottish players to Serie A has been the talk of it.

The exploits of Scott McTominay and Billy Gilmour at Napoli have been comprehensively documented. Che Adams is thriving at Torino where he now shares a dressing room with Nathan Patterson. You can count Kieron Bowie, Josh Doig, Lennon Miller and Liam Henderson among the diaspora, too.

However, another Scot’s switch to Italy has largely flown under the radar. Back in July, Jack Harper, the former Real Madrid wonderkid and presumed saviour of Scottish football, signed a one-year deal with ASD Nuova Igea Virtus.

Currently playing in Serie D, the fourth tier of the Italian national league pyramid, the Sicilian part-timers were founded in 1946 and subsequently re-founded in 1964, 2011 and again in 2019. Which is to say they’ve had a complicated existence.

Harper can surely relate. Now 30, the Malaga-born frontman was 13 when he first made headlines, signing with Real Madrid after impressing in a youth football tournament. He spent almost six years with Los Blancos, learning his trade in its exalted ‘La Fabrica’ academy under the watchful eye of top coaches, Fernando Morientes and Zinedine Zidane amongst them.

If he wasn’t bumping into Cristiano Ronaldo in the swimming pool, he was having a blether with Gareth Bale or studying Luka Modric. All the while, he was quietly developing, establishing himself as one of the top scorers in multiple age groups within the academy.

Jack Harper now plies his trade in Italy's Serie D with Sicilian club ASD Nuova Igea Virtus

Soon after his 18th birthday, and with Real’s youth structure under review, he decided to swap Madrid for Brighton, signing a two-year deal with the then English Championship side. He couldn’t have known it at the time, but Harper’s move to the Amex Stadium was the start of a frustratingly nomadic decade.

A catalogue of injuries and bad luck kick-started a footballing odyssey that has taken in spells at Malaga, Getafe, Alcorcón, Cartagena and Villarreal, as well as Racing Santander, Hércules, Marbella, Linense and, more recently, Spanish fourth-division outfit Linares.

Harper joined the latter ahead of the 2025-26 season and made an encouraging start, scoring four goals in his first nine appearances before, once again, injury struck. He spent almost four months on the sidelines and, when the campaign ended, he found himself a free agent once more.

‘At that point, I decided to forget all about it until after the World Cup,’ he tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘I said to my family I didn’t want to think about it. I needed to just disconnect.’

He and his brother Ryan travelled to Miami to take in Scotland’s final group match against Brazil and, standing shoulder to shoulder with the Tartan Army in the stands of the Hard Rock Stadium, he allowed himself to wonder what might have been.

‘It was definitely in the back of my mind that I could have been on the pitch because that’s the type of person I am,’ says Harper. ‘I know that if the road was a bit straighter and I’d had just a little more luck, then absolutely, I could have been there representing my country.

Harper had the world at his feet when he signed for Real Madrid at the tender age of 13

‘Years ago, I was knocking on the door when I was playing in Spain. I was called up to the 30-man squad several times but then the injuries started to hit and the door kind of closed. So yeah, of course I was at the stadium thinking I should have been playing. I know the level of football I’m capable of. I just never got a chance to show it.

‘But being there was a cool experience. The atmosphere was unbelievable and to see us taking on a Brazil side dressed in the yellow jerseys with those five stars on them, it was incredible. The World Cup’s the pinnacle of football. I was just glad to be part of it somehow.’

After that party in the US, Harper returned to Spain to discover he was a man in demand.

‘I had a few interesting offers on the table,’ he smiles. ‘I spoke with my partner and we agreed that, whilst our preference was to stay in Spain, it might be wise for us to consider all options. Last season was really hard and so we thought that maybe a change of scenery would do us all good.

‘Next thing I knew, I had an offer from a team in Iraq. There was an opportunity with a team in Thailand, too. That was very, very close to being done. But then an agent contacted me out of the blue with some deals from Italy. Soon enough, we were packing our bags and moving to Sicily.’

Despite the relative proximity of the two countries, Harper insists Spanish and Italian football could not be more different.

Harper rubbed shoulders with the game's leading lights in Spain, including Cristiano Ronaldo

Zinedine Zidane was just beginning his coaching career during Harper's time at the Bernabeu

‘It’s been a bit of a culture shock,’ he admits. ‘Football in Italy is much more physical. I don’t think I touched a ball for the first ten days of pre-season. It was all about getting fit and not worrying about the technical side of things.

‘It’s different, but that’s why I’m here. I needed to get out of my comfort zone. I feel like I’ve got it all to prove. Nobody really knows me here, I don’t know the language... it’s not easy.

‘But maybe that’s what I need. You know, thirty’s still young. I could have another decade-plus of playing in front of me. So, the plan is to get fit, stay fit and hopefully start climbing the leagues again. The hunger is still there.’

He adds: ‘I’ve kind of been on an opposite journey to a lot of people. I started at a huge club, maybe the biggest club in the world; I’ve had a good contract with a La Liga team; I’ve played in front of my hometown fans and heard them chanting my name. So, I know what it’s like to be there. It doesn’t scare me in the slightest. I’ve had a taste of it and I’m hungry for more.

‘Cristiano Ronaldo has shown how long it’s possible to stay at the top level. So, too, Karim Benzema. Even Harry Kane. What is he now, 33? And he’s just had the best year of his career, winning the Ballon d’Or. It’s not that long ago people were writing forwards off at that age. So, no, I’m still motivated and I don’t see any reason why, with a wee bit of luck, I can’t keep playing until I’m close to my forties.’

If Harper’s self-belief and resilience sound impressive, it’s because he’s had ample opportunity to work on them. In addition to his various injury issues, he’s had to contend with the weight of expectation that comes with being on the books of Real Madrid, intense scrutiny from a very young age, and, of course, plenty of rejection.

Harper moved to Brighton in 2015 but his career failed to take flight with the Seagulls

Perhaps the most memorable example of the latter came in 2015 when he was left out of the Scotland Under-19 squad by then-coach Ricky Sbragia. The former Sunderland boss triggered a backlash from former players, fans and pundits alike when he dismissed Harper as ‘a luxury player’ that his team couldn’t accommodate.

Spanish football journalist Graham Hunter described it as a ‘retrograde, almost prehistoric decision’. Harper’s dad, John, branded the description ‘harsh’, warning that Scotland could lose his son to the Spanish national team.

Sbragia subsequently apologised for his choice of words but Harper admits it took him some time to get over.

‘It was hard to deal with,’ he nods, ‘especially considering the love I have for Scotland. I might have been born in Spain, but I’ve got Scottish blood pumping through me. Honestly, the prospect of playing for Scotland was always more exciting to me than playing for Real Madrid. But that was just the mentality some people had at that time.

‘I was probably the most high-profile victim of that way of thinking but there would have been others as well, players who maybe weren’t as physical and so were written off. But I would definitely say times have changed. You can see that with more technical players like Billy Gilmour coming through and being successful.

‘The game has moved on from that kind of thinking and it’s a good thing, I think, for Scotland that it has.’

Harper, in action for Getafe, has played for a host of Spanish clubs and wanted a new challenge

Whilst his international experience amounts to a handful of age-grade caps, Harper has not yet given up on playing again for his country.

‘The beautiful thing about football is that things can change quickly, especially if you’re a striker. You only need a season or a season and a half of scoring goals, and your career can lift off again. There are so many examples of that, maybe now more than ever.

‘So, that’s the thing that keeps me motivated every day when I go to training. If I can get into a good rhythm, score goals and stay fit, then who knows what might happen? I still have that dream and that hunger to play for Scotland. That might seem a bit crazy to some people. Honestly, sometimes it even seems a bit crazy to me. But it’s the thing that drives me and it’ll continue to drive me either until it happens or I retire.’

Harper admits he would love to experience playing in Scotland before he hangs up his boots, having come close to doing so on multiple occasions in the past.

‘I’ve had phone calls where it’s been like, “Okay, it’s going to get done” and then, for one reason or another, it hasn’t happened,’ he says. ‘I came pretty close to joining St Johnstone one time, and Falkirk as well many years ago. The last couple of years, there’s been interest from some Championship sides. It’s a challenge I’m definitely up for and something I’d like to make happen.’

#1328. Could chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Tammy Worth is a freelance health-care reporter in Kansas City, Missouri.

Potential links between pesticide exposure and health problems are hard to tease out.Credit: brt COMM/Alamy

In May, Vermont became the first US state to pass legislation that bans most uses of paraquat, a chemical herbicide linked to an increased risk of Parkinson’s disease. Other states have also examined paraquat’s safety. California’s Department of Pesticide Regulation studied the chemical in 2024, but chose not to ban it. However, in August, after persistent advocacy from farm workers and environmental groups, the state announced plans to phase out paraquat over a two-year period.

Paraquat is already banned in 70 countries, including China, Brazil, Turkey and member states of the European Union (where it’s been prohibited for nearly 20 years). And paraquat isn’t the only chemical under scrutiny. Other pesticides have been identified as potential triggers of Parkinson’s disease, including the heavy metals; the fish poison rotenone and the solvent trichloroethylene (TCE), which used in dry cleaning.

Although many researchers are certain that environmental factors play a fundamental part in Parkinson’s risk, they have struggled to convince regulators, particularly at the US federal level. Population studies take decades to complete, and the interplay between environmental toxicants and individuals’ genetic risk is difficult to tease out. But many neurologists and Parkinson’s advocates think that the science is sufficient to link some chemicals to the condition.

The delay in regulatory action is not caused by a lack of research, says Beate Ritz, an epidemiologist at the Fielding School of Public Health at the University of California, Los Angeles. “You can pile on as much science as you want to; it won’t change a thing until there is political will.”

It’s widely accepted that Parkinson’s disease is linked to a combination of factors, including genetics, changes to the brain as it ages and environmental triggers.

Genetics might be the most well-understood factor. About 20 gene variants have been linked to Parkinson’s. These variants are thought to cause the accumulation of proteins that clump to form Lewy bodies — aggregations that damage dopamine-producing nerve cells and deplete the brain’s supply of this ‘feel-good’ neurotransmitter. The loss of dopamine affects the brain’s ability to control movement.

But genetics accounts for only about 5–15% of cases of Parkinson’s disease. Other causes include behavioural factors such as physical activity, diet and smoking. Head trauma, some medications and even having red hair (because of a mutation in the MC1R gene) could also increase risk.

The potential link between chemicals and Parkinson’s was discovered in the early 1980s. Neurologist William Langston and his colleagues at the Santa Clara Valley Medical Center in San José, California, found that a small number of people who had taken a synthetic opioid called MPTP exhibited Parkinson’s-like symptoms1. Langston noted that when MPTP entered the brain, it was quickly converted to the toxic metabolite MPP+, which damages dopamine-producing neurons and is structurally similar to chemicals such as paraquat.

There’s seldom a one-to-one correlation between a toxicant and the development of Parkinson’s, says Rebecca Gilbert, a neurologist specializing in Parkinson’s disease and chief mission officer of the New York City-based American Parkinson Disease Association. She says it’s rare that someone’s Parkinson’s can be traced directly to them playing on their grandfather’s farm that was sprayed with paraquat when they were seven years old. Instead, it’s typically an amalgam of several risk factors. “I picture it like a glass of water,” Gilbert says. “You pour in that exposure to the spraying when you were seven, and then you pour in genetics, and then you pour in a little TCE.”

Part of the challenge of deciphering how different chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s disease is that much of the damage occurs slowly, long before a person is diagnosed. And during those years, other factors can modify disease progression — making it difficult to pinpoint which exposures matter.

Study participants can’t be exposed to pollutants deliberately, so scientists seeking to establish that association are left with epidemiological and animal studies. But epidemiological studies take decades, and no country has an official registry of people with Parkinson’s disease for researchers to contact. And animal studies can’t completely mimic either the age-related loss of dopamine-producing brain cells or the full range of Parkinson’s symptoms.

Ray Dorsey, a neurologist at the Atria Health and Research Institute in New York City, studies environmental triggers of Parkinson’s. In work published in 2023, he highlighted a handful of case studies of people who developed Parkinson’s after TCE exposure2. One of these looked at 99 pairs of twins and found that exposure to TCE increased the risk of Parkinson’s by more than 500%. “We’re paying a really high price for dry-cleaning things,” Dorsey says.

One of the most well-known epidemiological studies of Parkinson’s involved military personnel stationed at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina. In 1982, the US Marine Corps found that water on the base was contaminated with volatile organic compounds, most notably TCE. A study3 published in 2023 focused on the health conditions of people who had been at Camp Lejeune for at least three months between 1975 and 1985. When researchers followed up these individuals between 1997 and 2021, they found that their rate of Parkinson’s disease was 70% higher than it was among personnel who had been living at Camp Pendelton, California — where the water was not contaminated — for at least three months during that same ten-year period3. Even among the Camp Lejeune veterans who did not have Parkinson’s, there was a higher prevalence of symptoms that might pre-date a Parkinson’s diagnosis, such as constipation, tremors and loss of sense of smell.

Use of the weedkiller paraquat has been linked to Parkinson’s disease.Credit: Romeo Gacad/AFP via Getty

Ritz uses geographical information system modelling to track environmental exposures and their link to conditions such as Parkinson’s. One of her focuses is farming communities. In a study published in 2024, she and her colleagues analysed people living or working near three agricultural counties in central California where farms were treated with paraquat4. The data went back to 1974, and peoples’ exposure times ranged from about 8 to 30 years. The researchers found that having higher exposure at work or at home increased the chance of getting Parkinson’s by 91%.

It’s intuitive to study people living and working in farming communities because of their direct contact with chemicals and the ability to track which products are used. But Dorsey co-authored a 2025 paper that found that the risk could extend to a wider population5. The study tracked people living near golf courses in Minnesota and Wisconsin. The researchers compared a 5,113-person control group and 419 people with Parkinson’s and found that living within 1.6 kilometres of a golf course raised the chance of getting Parkinson’s by 126%, compared with the risk for people who lived at least 9.6 kilometres away. The researchers also observed that this risk dropped the farther away people lived. The authors posited that the increased risk close by could be due to exposure to pesticides through inhalation and groundwater. Researchers didn’t measure the types or levels of pesticides, but noted that they are frequently used on golf courses, particularly in the United States, which uses as much as 15 times more pesticides on golf courses than do European countries.

“It shouldn’t be terribly surprising,” Dorsey says, “that chemicals designed to damage the nervous system of insects might have similar consequences on the nervous system of humans.”

Rotenone is another pesticide that could contribute to Parkinson’s. But there are few human studies that link it to the condition. One commonly cited study from 2011 compared 110 people with Parkinson’s (mostly farmers) who had formerly applied restricted-use pesticides on private property and a control group of 358 people from Iowa and North Carolina who regularly used chemicals at work in the 1990s, but were not cognitively impaired or diagnosed with Parkinson’s. Researchers found that people who had worked with rotenone — which degrades the function of mitochondria — had a 2.5 times higher risk of developing Parkinson’s than did people in the control group6. More-recent animal studies lend credence to this link. A 2025 study found that rats exposed to rotenone for 21 days had dysfunction in motor cortex synapses and upregulation of C1q (a glycoprotein) in the substantia nigra, a part of the brain that is affected in Parkinson’s7. This increased activity suggests an inflammatory response in that region of the brain.

For Parkinson’s researchers, chemicals linked to the condition can’t be banned quickly enough. But regulators in the United States seem more hesitant than their counterparts in many other countries.

The European Union banned TCE a decade ago. The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) released a review of TCE in 2024 that prohibited its use in consumer products and many industrial and commercial products as of 15 September 2025. There are exceptions for some applications, however, including one lasting 50 years for what the EPA calls “essential laboratory use”.

Paraquat is undergoing review by the EPA, in a process conducted on regulated pesticides at least every 15 years. The agency has requested more data from manufacturers, and has said that it will host a roundtable to solicit public input.

Rotenone is banned in the European Union and the United Kingdom, but continues to be used in the United States and Canada to control invasive fish populations.

“The EPA demands an absurd level of proof that something is dangerous,” says Tim Greenamyre, a neurologist at the University of Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania. “They don’t like epidemiological studies,” he says, but they also “throw out animal studies because they say toxicants aren’t given at the exact dose that humans get”.

Greenamyre has a personal stake in this issue. He studied rotenone in his lab for decades and was himself diagnosed with Parkinson’s in 2021. Because of the lack of research on chemical causes of the disease, he says, any connection between his exposure and his diagnosis would only be speculative. But he hopes to help fill that gap in knowledge: he has received funding to study the mechanism by which rotenone, TCE and paraquat might trigger Parkinson’s.

Another open question is how many other chemicals might cause damage to the brain similar to that in Parkinson’s. Ritz’s current research is focusing on organophosphates and organochlorides, but she says there are many other potential offenders, including carbamates, pyrethroids and neonicotinoids — all pesticides.

Researchers such as Ritz have access to pesticide report systems that record who is spraying which chemical, where and when. But by the time they finish studying one pesticide, it has been replaced with a different one, which is later replaced by yet another.

“We are basically 20–30 years behind what’s happening in the fields,” Ritz says. And with every new contaminant that enters the scene, the potential that one might trigger Parkinson’s ticks up a notch.

#1327. Serie A Liveblog: Roma-Sassuolo, Parma-Bologna, Cagliari-Frosinone, Torino-Lecce

Join us for all the build-up and action from today’s four Serie A games, building up to Roma vs. Sassuolo, after Cagliari-Frosinone, Torino-Lecce and local derby Parma vs. Bologna.

We begin at 14.00 GMT (15.00 CET) with high-flying Frosinone visiting Cagliari and Torino up against Lecce, then at 17.00 GMT (18.00 CET) there’s the Emilia-Romagna Derby at the Stadio Tardini.

At 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET), Roma try to shake off the Manchester United debacle and keep up in the Scudetto race against Alberto Aquilani’s Sassuolo.

Roma made short work of sorry Sassuolo with Mario Hermoso, an own goal and Rodrigo Mora, inflicting a fifth consecutive defeat on Alberto Aquilani’s side.

Fali Cande’ on for Sassuolo, Caleta-Car off.

It’s still all Roma, Pisilli strike charged down in the box!

Pisilli breaks down the left and cuts inside, right-foot finish to force a save out of Muric at the near post!

Castro and Koulierakis on, Malen and Hermoso off

Malen dribbles down the left, gets around Muric, but doesn’t get enough power or precision on the pull-back, allowing Caleta-Car to clear in the six-yard box!

Lipani and Adzic on, Thorstvedt and Sebastiano Esposito off for Sassuolo.

Nahuel Molina runs down the right and his angled drive goes wide, partly due to pressure from Caleta-Car.

Pisilli and De Roon on for Roma, Kone and Rodrigo Mora off.

Sudden Sassuolo strike from distance, but also well wide of the target from Sulemana.

Malen involved again, completing the give and go with Mora to drill through Caleta-Car’s legs into the far bottom corner from 14 yards!

Malen sent through by Hermoso, but Muric parries the central strike!

Roma continue to not score, pull-back from the right for Kone, desperate interception from a Sassuolo defender, then Mora attempt charged down too.

Malen into the box again, this time he fires wide onto the side-netting.

Soule’ runs onto a through ball, dribbles around the goalkeeper, could score into an empty net, instead tries to roll it across for Malen, who isn’t expecting it and falls over because his body is in the wrong position…

Sassuolo scrap the 3-5-2 formation, then.

Bowie and Van Der Brempt on for Sassuolo, Matic and Cinquegrano off.

Mikel Arteta has praised Noni Madueke’s response to a difficult start to the season after the winger played another decisive role in Arsenal’s 1-0 victory over Hull City.

Martin Odegaard scored the only goal at the Emirates Stadium after 72 minutes, reacting quickest when Kostas Tzolakis saved Madueke’s effort.

Arsenal were far from their fluent best, but the victory moved the defending champions six points clear at the top of the Premier League.

As reported by Arsenal News, Arteta believes Madueke has transformed his performances after responding positively to limited playing time earlier in the campaign.

Arteta said of Madueke: “That’s the second part of the story – the first is that you need to earn the right to be able to do that.

“Noni did that, he reacted to not playing often, went away, started to train and was a different Noni.

“He wasn’t going to accept that situation, he meant business, and since then he has been incredible.

“Now you are in that position, he needs to hone and improve it, so let’s see if he can do that.”

Madueke was Arsenal’s most dangerous attacker against Hull, registering five successful dribbles and creating several opportunities.

Sky Sports also reports that he is now averaging 3.57 chances created per 90 minutes, the highest rate of any Premier League player this season.

Madueke’s improvement could be particularly important while Bukayo Saka is unavailable.

Earlier in the season, a January exit was even being discussed. CaughtOffside reported in September that Atletico Madrid and Juventus were monitoring his situation after his limited Premier League involvement.

That possibility now feels considerably less likely.

Madueke has responded exactly how Arteta would have wanted: rather than becoming frustrated, he worked independently during the international break and returned sharper. His passing accuracy, crossing and dribble success have all improved compared with last season.

There is still one obvious area to improve. Madueke had chances to score against Hull and could have made the victory far more comfortable.

But Arsenal now have a winger who is creating chances at an elite rate and increasingly influencing important matches. If he can add more ruthless finishing, Arteta may soon face a genuine selection dilemma when Saka returns.

#1325. Bayern Munich's £400,000-a-week 'risk' on Harry Kane: Dietmar Hamann reveals doubts about Ballon d'Or winner - and claims no English team would have matched mega contract offer

Published: 17:12 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 17:12 EDT, 6 November 2026

Bayern Munich are taking a major 'risk' giving Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane a bumper new deal, according to former midfielder Didi Hamann.

Kane, 33, and Bayern Munich have agreed on a two-year contract extension worth £400,000 per week which will make him the world's highest-paid English sportsman.

But ex-Liverpool and Bayern man Hamann has suggested that this may prove to be a poor move given Kane's age and possible decline.

'Whether he'll still be scoring goals in the coming years, we'll see. He's 33 years old and will be 36 when the contract expires. There's obviously a certain risk involved,' Champions League winner Hamann told Sky Germany.

Hamann then went on to justify his bizarre comments by saying: 'He didn't play well for England at the European Championship two years ago, and he had problems in the last two knockout matches at the World Cup.'

The ex-Germany international also suggested that staying at Bayern was the best deal Kane was going to get at this stage in his career, saying: 'I don't think there were any major suitors from England.

Harry Kane has signed a two-year-long contract extension with Bayern but Didi Hamann is not convinced this is the right move for the Bavarians

Speaking with Sky Germany Dietmar Hamann expressed concerns over his old side offering Kane such a large deal

'They would have taken him for 20 or 30 million, but Bayern would probably have wanted at least half or three-quarters back this summer of the 100 million euros they had to pay Tottenham for Kane in 2023.

'I don't think anyone would have paid that. That's why the contract extension is something they probably couldn't have done any differently.'

Hamann is arguably taking a harsh view on Kane's new deal considering how the Englishman has performed since arriving in Germany.

In three seasons at the Allianz he has 102 Bundesliga goals in as many games as well as 28 assists, winning the Bundesliga Golden Boot every year since his arrival.

The Englishman's goals have fired Bayern to two back-to-back Bundesliga titles and a DFB-Pokal triumph.

But clearly all of this is not enough for Hamann who has previously critiqued Kane's performances in Germany saying that last season his role in Kompany's Bayern side was 'unacceptable.'

In his Sky Germany column the former defensive midfielder wrote: 'I don't know if Kompany is happy that Harry Kane is no longer playing exclusively as a striker.

'It's not acceptable to me that Kane is winning balls in his own penalty area, because that's not his job at all.'

#1324. Orsolini praise for Bologna coach Palladino is damning for Tedesco

Bologna won their fourth game in a row under new coach Raffaele Palladino, as Riccardo Orsolini pins the blame on sacked Domenico Tedesco. ‘We’re enjoying ourselves again.’

The Rossoblu had got off to a truly disastrous start under former Belgium international coach Tedesco, scraping one point from the opening four Serie A matches.

All three defeats were 1-0 scorelines, and he was fired on September 16 to bring in Palladino.

It has been a complete transformation, drawing the opener and then winning five of the next six games, faltering only 3-1 to Inter.

“The coach arrived in a bit of a rush, because we had started so badly and there was no time to discuss too much,” Orsolini told DAZN Italia after today’s 2-1 win away to Parma, their fourth on the bounce.

“We had to win games, he did well to get us all on the same page and bring us back together, seeing as this was a team that had done well over the years. We lost some important players over the summer, but the skeleton of that team remained.”

When Orsolini had praise for Palladino, he namechecked several previous Bologna bosses too, but notably left Tedesco out of the list.

“I’ve been here for many years and went through a lot of different situations. I enjoyed myself with Thiago Motta, with Vincenzo Italiano, and now we are enjoying ourselves again with Palladino.

“I don’t know how far this team can go, but we want to enjoy ourselves together. We rediscovered our smile.”

Bologna are climbing back up the table after four consecutive victories against Cagliari, Milan, Monza and Parma, but notably three of those were away from home.

This was Orsolini’s second goal of the season in just five appearances, as it was his comeback from almost a month out with a thigh injury.

#1323. When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Emma Marris is a writer in Portland, Oregon.

Life-sized puppets in a remote village in Japan symbolize depopulation in the country. Credit: Buddhika Weerasinghe/Getty

Less than an hour’s train ride from central Tokyo, ecologist Kei Uchida walks through glades of mountain cherry trees and meadows filled with susuki grass as tall as an elephant. The researcher smiles when he spots something by the trail: a tangled orb of grass stalks, at about knee height. It is the nest of the tiny Eurasian harvest mouse (Micromys minutus), a species that has been on the decline in this area and has been targeted for protection.

Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them

Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them

Volunteers saved this location around Mount Tenran from development 30 years ago, and today they monitor its plants and animals, thin its forests and even plant and harvest rice — all in the name of biodiversity. Here, nature needs people. In the shallow water of the rice paddy, fish as small and arched as an eyebrow swim, and just above the water’s surface, dragonflies mate. At dusk, fireflies dance above the fields.

Uchida, an environmental scientist at Tokyo City University in Yokohama, and his colleagues included this site in a study of thousands of species in more than 150 wooded, agricultural and ‘peri-urban’ landscapes in Japan1. Unsurprisingly, they found that the diversity and abundance of most species declined at sites where the human population was growing. But they also found that biodiversity declined in places where the number of people was decreasing (see ‘Lost life’). This result — and others like it in different parts of the world — contradicts the common assumption that when people leave, nature always thrives.

Japan and many other nations are seeing a vast emptying of rural areas as people flock towards urban centres. Studies2 are showing that this can have a detrimental effect on biodiversity in the depopulated areas, which creates new challenges. Rather than simply setting up and managing protected areas, conservation officials must consider whether and how to recruit, train and support people to be permanent parts of some ecosystems.

I’ve joined Uchida and local volunteers to learn more about how human activity can increase biodiversity. Uchida says that this area is a typical satoyama landscape — a term that combines the words for village and mountain. “Agriculture and living things can coexist,” Uchida says. But Japan’s satoyama are being lost to depopulation and urbanization.

In this area near Mount Tenran, as in many woodlands across Japan, humans spent centuries cutting trees for fuel and removing fallen leaves for fertilizer. That opened up the forest and benefited specific plants and insects. But when that activity stopped, the forest became dense and closed in again. “We have used the woods for 1,000 years, but not lately,” Uchida says. Now, young students are being given small handsaws and taught the centuries-old art of woodland thinning.

Kojima Tsubasa, a volunteer nature monitor, shows me where he sits in the evenings to count fireflies. There are two types here: the smaller heike fireflies (Aquatica lateralis), which prefer rice fields; and the larger, brighter genji fireflies (Nipponoluciola cruciata), associated with running streams. “It’s rare to see both at once,” he says, proudly. Four days ago, Tsubasa says, he counted 60 fireflies at this paddy. Often, he is not alone. Japanese urbanites, yearning for the charm of the countryside, come here to watch the fireflies at dusk. But after the show, they get on the train and return to the brighter lights of Tokyo.

Most Japanese people now have to travel to see fireflies — whereas once the insect’s bright beauty was right outside their homes. It’s a trend seen the world over. As recently as 1950, nearly 40% of the global human population lived in the countryside. According to United Nations data, just 19% of the world’s 8.2 billion people now live in rural areas. The global rural population is expected to peak in the 2040s and decline thereafter.

In some countries, that rural decline is well under way. Japan’s total population shrank by four million between 2015 and 2025, and the rural population is shrinking even faster. In 2025, just 8.6% of its population was classified as rural. Peter Matanle, an independent environmental social scientist who worked with Uchida on the biodiversity study, calls Japan a “vanguard country” that other nations can learn from when it comes to depopulation. European Union data, for example, show that between 2015 and 2024, rural areas in Europe lost 0.2% of their population per year. Furthermore, rural communities tend to have older populations than do urban communities, a harbinger of further depopulation.

Uchida and his co-authors studied the effects of this demographic shift by examining data on 464 species of bird, butterfly, firefly and frog as well as nearly 3,000 plant species collected in various landscapes across Japan over periods of 5–17 years, starting in 2004. They found that biodiversity declined in areas where there was greater disruption of the landscape — either by people moving in and building infrastructure or by agricultural intensification, in which corporate farms replace smaller, family-run operations.

Rewilding the planet: how seven artificial islands could help a dying Dutch lake

Rewilding the planet: how seven artificial islands could help a dying Dutch lake

They also documented declines in biodiversity in places abandoned by people. Although that might seem paradoxical, the researchers note that when irrigation ceases, amphibians and many insects can no longer reproduce; other ecological niches are lost as well. The resulting dry, abandoned landscape is too fragmented for many species to recolonize. “Leaving it alone isn’t doing anyone any good,” Matanle says.

Similar relationships between rural depopulation and biodiversity have been documented in Europe. A study of 70 sites in Albania, Bulgaria, Croatia and Greece found that rural abandonment in these countries had “a consistent negative effect on bird communities”2. The species hit hardest were those that populate farmlands, according to the researchers. A European Commission monitoring scheme found that populations of farmland birds in Europe declined by 58% between 1980 and 2024, as agriculture intensified in some locations and moved out of others.

Birds are not the only organisms that have thrived in human landscapes. In Sweden, ‘semi-natural grasslands’, which have been cleared by humans and are kept open by livestock, are prime habitat for one-third of the country’s threatened species, and can contain up to 40 plant species per square metre3. As people left the countryside after the Second World War and land use evolved away from extensive pastures, the total area of these grasslands decreased by more than 90% in some regions4. In many cases, the removal of grazers led to the land being converted to row crops or forest — due to either spontaneous growth of trees or intentional planting for timber. Both types of forest are less biodiverse than the semi-natural grasslands they replaced.

In Spain, ecologist Francisco Lloret, at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, says that as people leave the countryside, biodiversity falls because some species are losing habitat and others are losing food. Vultures and other scavengers, for example, have relied on livestock for centuries, but that source of food is disappearing.

A revolution is sweeping Europe’s farms: can it save agriculture?

A revolution is sweeping Europe’s farms: can it save agriculture?

Wooded or herbaceous areas on the edges of fields are also in decline. In Mediterranean countries such as Spain, fields are often bounded by herbaceous borders — or by dry stone walls, which shelter many vertebrates and invertebrates. When such walls are knocked down to make larger fields for modern agricultural systems that require fewer people, those organisms are lost.

Why do so many species thrive in low-intensity farming landscapes? The mechanisms behind the relationship vary from species to species, say researchers. Some organisms prefer the standing water of rice fields, some tend towards the grasslands kept open by mowing or livestock, and some thrive at the edge of a forest. But the overarching themes of research seem to be that many species rely on the maintenance of a mosaic of habitat types and regular, modest disturbance through activities such as seasonal flooding, livestock grazing, burning, thinning and patchy clearing. Inhabited landscapes that experience such disruptions often host more species than a large expanse of undisturbed forest does.

These are the Arcadian landscapes of the Romantic poets, of The Wind in the Willows (1908) and of My Neighbor Totoro: culturally beloved ecosystems that have supported a suite of species since at least the Iron Age. “Biodiversity has evolved in the last millennia with people and human activities,” Lloret says. Some species might even have evolved to fit better into human landscapes. However, Lloret cautions that there are no universal rules. Context is king. In some places, depopulation increases biodiversity. Top predators, such as wolves, often do best in places without people. In the tropics — home to the most biodiverse places on Earth — few countries are experiencing depopulation and habitat loss is a much greater concern.

In response to biodiversity losses linked to rural depopulation, a team of conservation researchers in the Czech Republic and Poland have called for small-scale farming as a conservation tool to save farmland birds5. As a bonus, such farming communities would provide “high aesthetic and heritage values”, the team argues. Uchida and his colleagues suggest “a new interventionist wilding” to complement rewilding efforts that seek to set up nature to run itself. Some schemes run by the EU aim to support farmers and biodiversity, but they’ve been criticized as being ineffective6.

After my hike with the volunteers and Uchida, we emerge from the forest just as the sky opens and rain begins to pour. We go to a nearby bakery for a Japanese snack called curry bread, and I ask the question that has been on my mind all day: who will do the work of creating habitats for vulnerable species in the countryside in the future?

#1322. Martin O'Neill relaxed over Kasper Hogh scoring drought as Celtic boss hails Dane's display against Besiktas

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EDT, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 17:30 EDT, 6 November 2026

Martin O'Neill is adamant that he’s not overly concerned about Kasper Hogh’s goal drought — despite the Dane failing to find the net in 15 matches.

Celtic’s record signing at £11million from Bodo/Glimt, the forward looked set to be a huge hit when he scored a hat-trick at Kilmarnock on August 9 only to go off the boil.

His hopes of ending a barren run against Besiktas on Thursday ended when he was taken off 13 minutes from time, with substitutes Callum Osmand and Camilo Duran climbing off the bench to seal a dramatic 3-2 for O’Neill’s men.

But while O’Neill shared Hogh’s frustration at not getting among the goals again, he made a point of telling him that he should have been proud of his other work on the night.

‘I did, absolutely,’ he explained. ‘I want centre-forwards to be able to hold it and that is what he did.

‘He is not Duran, he is not a dribbler. But if he can do this for us against strong opposition it will stand him in good stead.’

O'Neill admits his record-signing is currently struggling for confidence in front of goal

Hogh hasn't found the net since firing a hat-trick in a 5-1 win over Kilmarnock on August 9

With his player not in the latest Denmark squad, O’Neill believes confidence may be an issue. But he stressed: ‘I think Thursday night will be good for him. I said to him that I’m not worried about whether he scores a goal.

‘Of course, you want centre-forwards to score and, of course, centre-forwards live on them. But I said to him that last night I wanted him to be strong and fight when the ball is played up to him.

'I thought in terms of holding the ball up and bringing people into the game, that he did really well.’

Duran stole the headlines against the Turks, though, with his double securing Celtic’s first win in the Europa League and bringing his personal tally for the season to 13.

‘At this minute, he is on fire,’ O’Neill said of the Colombian. ‘He can play wide right, he has done that. He has played wide left for his other club. But centre forward is where he is dynamic.’

Asked if it was increasingly difficult to start Hogh ahead of Duran through the middle, O’Neill said: ‘We will see. We made five changes on Thursday night because it was necessary.

‘Centre-forwards need a goal but that performance there against European opposition will give him confidence.

‘I don’t know what side we will play on Sunday. But this lad has scored goals in the Champions League remember.

'He will get a confidence boost from Thursday night in terms of doing that part of the game well. But it will be nice for him to score a goal.’

While O’Neill’s side now focus on Kilmarnock, the win over Besiktas has breathed new life into their European campaign. With three points on the board at the midway point, two further wins from their matches with Torreense, Omonia, Marseille and Union Saint-Gilloise may see them qualify for the knockout round.

‘It was really pleasing and really important,’ O’Neill said of Thursday’s dramatic victory. ‘We conceded some ground in the game which was to be expected, but I thought defensively we were really, really strong.

‘From the European side, we have given ourselves a chance. We will have to go and win away from home and it will not be easy. We are looking forward to Sunday and we will look to take it on.’

#1321. Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

Johan Manzambi heads Aston Villa in front! 🟣 https://t.co/jxZf2568Sl

It is getting hard to comprehend what Jaissle wants his team to do. The much-hyped “vertical” style looks like an ugly incarnation of the long ball football of yesteryear. They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. Newcastle are not getting better; they are making all the same mistakes and, if anything, as an attacking force, they are looking increasingly stale and predictable. They did not have a shot on target in the first half and, other than one fantastic save in the second, Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki had nothing to do.

"If he doesn't slip Harvey Barnes in, he's got to hit the target" Shay Given discusses Newcastle's decision-making in the final third 🔲 https://t.co/wh4kCAEbxV

“Our decision-making in the final third was lacking today,” Jaissle said. “I am frustrated, I understand the supporters’ reaction, that is their right [to boo after a defeat at home].”

It is time for a sharp dose of medicine on Tyneside. Expectations need to be adjusted, especially as none of the new signings have impressed. This was always the fear and the risk when you put all your faith in young players from abroad.

For Jaissle’s vertical football to work, Newcastle need to be able to win the ball high up the pitch, whether that is with a high press or competing for second balls from long passes. They do not do either well. More worryingly, they look so vulnerable, so easy to play through.

Villa did it to them all afternoon. Nicolas Jackson should have scored in the first half, Ibrahim Mbaye should have hit the target in the second.

On another day, Newcastle could also have had centre-back Sven Botman sent off for a lunge on Jackson. Then it really would have become ugly, but the Dutchman survived a VAR check.

Villa were always the better side. There was no fluency in Newcastle’s game, no structure, no patterns of play. Every time they turned over the ball, they looked stretched. Every time they got a set-piece, it was defended easily. Every time they went forward in the first half, the ball was sent aimlessly long and came straight back at them. #1320. Serie A probable line-ups: Napoli vs. Lazio

Serie A leaders Lazio are forced to do without Mattia Zaccagni, but rely on Davide Frattesi and Gustav Isaksen, while Napoli hope Kevin De Bruyne, Scott McTominay and Rasmus Hojlund can end the crisis.

It kicks off at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona in Naples on Sunday at 11.30 GMT (12.30 CET).

Few expected the two teams to be in their current position going into the season, as Gennaro Gattuso’s Lazio are alone three points clear at the top of the table, where Max Allegri is facing calls for his dismissal after a series of poor results, including the 4-1 Champions League defeat to FC Porto.

The injury crisis keeps on getting worse for Napoli, as Giovanni Di Lorenzo, Leonardo Spinazzola, Stanislav Lobotka, Benoit Badiashile, David Neres, Alisson Santos, Costantino Favasuli and Alessandro Buongiorno are ruled out.

Luca Marianucci is also suspended following his red card in last week’s 2-0 Serie A defeat to Juventus, with Mathias Olivera not at 100 per cent.

This leaves extremely limited options, so Allegri has two major choices to make over his tactical set-up.

It’s possible he could use a 3-5-2 with McTominay or De Bruyne pushed into a more advanced role in support of lone striker Hojlund, placing Matteo Politano and Antonio Vergara as the wing-backs.

Another alternative is getting Olivera on the left, with Vergara on the right, then using Noa Lang as the support for Hojlund, which would place both De Bruyne and McTominay in midfield.

Lazio have been without Albert Gudmundsson for several weeks, but the new absentee is captain Zaccagni with a thigh injury.

This does force a change for Gattuso, so Tijjani Noslin is expected to shuffle over into that wide role, leaving the centre-forward position to Andrea Pinamonti.

There are also some concerns over Nuno Tavares, who is struggling with a muscular issue, so Alfonso Pedraza is ready to step in if required at left-back.

Frattesi should take the midfield reins with Reda Belahyane and Kenneth Taylor, the only doubt is between Oliver Provstgaard and Diogo Leite in defence.

Lazio: Mandas; Floriani Mussolini, Sutalo, Provstgaard, Nuno Tavares; Frattesi, Belahyane, Taylor; Isaksen, Pinamonti, Noslin

#1319. Robbie Savage’s Reaction After Son, Charlie, Scores Against His Peterborough Team

Most FA Cup first-round ties come down to the usual storylines: giant-killings, rare TV coverage and a big pay day for the lower-league clubs.

Peterborough United against Reading had something far more personal going on. On the touchline was Posh boss Robbie Savage, and on the pitch was his son, as they came face-to-face in a professional setting.

Reading’s midfield boasted Charlie Savage, who has followed in his father's footsteps, having become a professional footballer in 2021, and he enjoyed a unique afternoon at the Weston Homes stadium in what was a rare start for the midfielder.

Before half-time, the plot had already taken a cruel turn for Savage senior, the former Wales international, as one side dominated on a cool and cloudy afternoon in the FA Cup First Round.

Savage was only appointed at Peterborough in October, and within weeks the draw had pitted him against the club where Charlie has played since leaving Manchester United in 2023.

The 52-year-old was open about how strange the build-up felt. He admitted that facing his son could be “horrible” and put their usual phone calls on hold, ensuring that Charlie wouldn’t accidentally let slip anything about Reading’s preparations.

“I will be consoling him or congratulating him,” Savage said of what would come after the final whistle.

The form guide only pointed one way, with Reading sixth in League One and Peterborough 22nd going into the tie, as one of the best stories of the round played out on Saturday afternoon.

Reading were already 2-0 up when Charlie struck in first-half stoppage time. His deflected effort found its way in for 3-0, in what was his first goal of the season, and he wheeled away to celebrate in front of the travelling Reading fans.

TNT Sports’ cameras quickly cut to the Peterborough dugout, where Savage was clearly torn between pride and the pain of watching his side go further behind.

Reaction on social media was interesting to say the least, with one fan saying: ‘He actually just looks like he’s buzzing his lad has scored but is pretending he’s p***** off.’ Another agreed: ‘He’s deffo pretending to be p***** off, he’s buzzing.’

Whilst others focused on how hard Savage was working to keep a straight face: ‘Trying his best not to be proud on the sidelines,’ wrote one. ‘He’s holding back everything he has not to smile,’ said another.

Another angle saw fans question the Peterborough boss’s acting skills, with one posting: ‘Look at manager pretending to be p***** lmfao.’

A second was even more blunt: ‘That's the worst bit of acting from Robbie trying to look angry.’

Reading added two more after the break to complete a 5-0 win at London Road, sending Charlie through to the second round and his father out of the competition.

Any pride Savage felt for his son was quickly overshadowed by his side’s display. Speaking afterwards, he called the defeat “embarrassing” and took the blame himself.

“I’m devastated. It’s not acceptable, it’s embarrassing,” he said. “It’s on me, I pick the players and I pick the tactics.”

It is a tough start to life in the dugout at Peterborough. Savage won his first game in charge against Leicester City, but Posh have now gone six matches without a win since.

For the Savage family, though, this is one afternoon that won’t be forgotten in a hurry, as this father-son duo have a professional moment in time to look back on, even if one will be happier than the other.
